title: 150 years ago, a mishap in an SA paddock revolutionised farming
text:
It has been 150 years since a mishap in a paddock led to a discovery that would forever change agriculture, but at the time the farmer-inventor was dismissed as a "fool and a lunatic".

Before 1876, one of the biggest challenges Mallee farmers faced was scrub stump.

Horse-drawn rollers and fire could flatten vegetation, but the stumps remained stubbornly in place, damaging the inflexible ploughs on the market.

Rollers were used to clear the hardy Mallee scrub. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

One day, Richard Smith, a blacksmith and farmer at Port Wakefield, was hard at work and broke part of his plough, according to Ardrossan Heritage Museum secretary Brenda Bowman.

"[He] realised through that accident that if the plough shear could move up and down, it could ride over obstacles," she said.

Richard and his brother, Clarence Smith, set about finessing a prototype that was to be unveiled at an exhibition at the Moonta Agricultural Show on November 6, 1876.

The first stump-jump plough was simple, but it would revolutionise Australian agriculture.

The museum contains many early designs of the plough. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Ploughing ahead

By attaching shears to the plough frame with a hinged joint and weight system, the plough could till soil without the scrub remnants being removed.

London-born Richard Bowyer Smith originated the stump-jump plough on the Yorke Peninsula. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

Despite addressing a common challenge, reactions to the invention were mixed.

"Some people thought it was a great idea and some people just thought it was lazy," said Ms Bowman, the widow of Clarence's great-grandson.

At the 1876 Moonta show, Richard Smith reportedly said: "I don't care what you say or think, I still firmly believe that my plough will open up a new agricultural era in South Australia."

Despite the scepticism the invention became commercially successful and in 1880 Clarence Smith opened a factory in Ardrossan.

The Clarence H. Smith plough factory employed up to 130 people at times, selling ploughs across the country and to New Zealand.

The factory opened by Clarence Smith traded until 1934. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Testimonials in a factory catalogue show just how pleased farmers were with the tool — a Mr John Baker called it "the most perfect plough ever offered".

"Four horses worked it all the season comfortably, and ploughed 220 acres of very rough stump and stony land without bending or breaking anything," he wrote.

The plough remained popular until the Great Depression saw the Ardrossan factory close in 1934.

Though much of it was demolished, part of the building remains and is now home to the Ardrossan Heritage Museum.

The Ardrossan Heritage Museum is home to many early designs and catalogues from the Smith brothers. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Unlocking Australia

In an 1881 paper, the president of the Royal Agricultural and Horticultural Society of SA Sir Robert Ross credited the plough with a drastic increase in farmed land.

Before the invention, scrubland was regularly forfeited by purchasers who found it "almost impossible" to farm.

"In 1873, 4,826 acres were leased, and more than half forfeited: in 1874, 2,183 acres were taken up, and all forfeited," Sir Ross wrote.

Stump-jump ploughs at the Ardrossan factory, as seen in an early catalogue. (Supplied: PIRSA)

As the use of the stump-jump plough increased, so did the amount of land leased, and 285,670 acres were purchased in 1881 in what was "the largest sale that has ever taken place in the colony".

"Both the Government and the farmers of South Australia are considerably indebted to Mr R B Smith for his ingenuity and perseverance in forcing this valuable implement upon the public," Sir Ross wrote.

" He was called a fool and a lunatic by his relations and neighbors, and, like many other inventors, instead of prospering by his invention, it has been his ruin. "

A sketch of the first single-furrow stump-jump plough by Richard Smith. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

A lapsed patent meant Richard Smith was not rewarded with riches for his invention, though in 1882 the state government awarded him £500 in recognition of the plough.

Richard and Clarence Smith ultimately had a falling out and Richard relocated to Western Australia.

The Royal Australian Mint has released a coin commemorating the plough. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Though farming machinery looks a little different these days, the principle of the stump-jump plough remains, but with more hydraulics.

This year, the Smith brothers' stump-jump plough featured alongside the jaffle maker and the black box flight recorder in a coin collection chronicling five of Australia's most decorated inventions.

title: Victoria's Big Build inquiry hears CFMEU threatened to 'smash' subcontractor
text:
Victoria's Big Build royal commission has heard a major contractor was wary of the "unprecedented access" the CFMEU had to government ministers, as well as alleged threats against subcontractors.

A level crossing removal project at Sunbury, in Melbourne's outer north, was the focus of the first day of a two-week block of public hearings.

The royal commission is exploring a number of themes, including allegations related to the conduct of the CFMEU (Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union) on sites.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Young KC noted that all of the themes being canvassed were allegations at this stage, some of which had been denied.

Contractor cautious of CFMEU's sway

Events related to a work stoppage at the Gap Road project in June 2022 were the focus of Monday's hearing.

Work ceased on June 6 and resumed on June 7 after control of the site was transferred to the CFMEU.

The commission heard that project costs blew out by an estimated $6 million.

Passages from several internal memos from site contractor John Holland were read out during today's hearing, including allegations about the CFMEU's relationship with the Victorian government.

Monday's hearing focused on the Gap Road level crossing removal at Sunbury in Melbourne's north. (Supplied: Victorian government)

"It is worth noting the significance of the CFMEU's relationship with the Andrews government in Victoria and the impact this is having and will have in the future in respect to client relationships," a memo dated to 2017 said.

"The union movement played a critical role in the election of the government, both organisationally and financially. The premier is factionally aligned with the Socialist Left and the CFMEU is the key industrial organisation in that faction.

"We also understand the CFMEU have unprecedented access to ministers and other key Victorian government stakeholders.

" We reasonably expect that the CFMEU in particular will have a substantial amount of knowledge around proposed government tenders and input in respect to the tender process. "

The commission heard that John Holland was increasingly cautious in its interactions with the CFMEU, with documents describing an escalating campaign by the union on the Gap Road site leading up to the June 2022 stop-work.

Big Build royal commission The construction sites of the Victorian government's Big Build have become hotbeds for allegations of criminal wrongdoing, corruption and serious misconduct.

CFMEU threatened to 'smash' subcontractor, commission hears

Allegations of threats of violence against subcontractors were also aired during today's hearing.

One instance was captured in notes from an internal contractor meeting about conduct on site ahead of the June 2022 stop-work.

"CFMEU are putting pressure on Wagstaff [Piling] not to work tonight, said 'you guys better not turn up tonight otherwise we'll smash you during the day'," Mr Young said, reading from a transcript.

The commission heard that police and WorkSafe Victoria were notified, but that Victoria Police took no action as it was regarded as an occupational health and safety issue.

Wagstaff Piling subsequently told firms they would not be working, citing pressure from the union.

The commission heard about events leading up to the June 2022 stop-work at Gap Road. (Supplied: Victorian government)

The commission heard similar incidents to those at the Gap Road project had played out at other Big Build sites.

"It is instructive that the commission has heard from other contractors with remarkably similar experience on other major projects," Mr Young said.

The royal commission has already received a raft of information, including private hearings and requests for more than 110,000 documents.

The hearings come as Victorians prepare to head to the polls for the November 28 state election.

Premier Ben Carroll today denied any knowledge of the CFMEU's access to senior government officials and ministers.

"What today's hearings show is that I am a premier that will make the tough decisions," Mr Carroll said.

title: How Nvidia came to investigate its CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
text:
The chief executive of Nvidia, the world's most valuable company and a close ally of US President Donald Trump, has admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who heads the tech giant that dominates the world's AI chip industry, sent a memo to staff acknowledging the affair after reports emerged the woman worked for China's Ministry of State Security.

Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into whether Mr Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

What has been reported?

The story centres on the Nvidia chief executive's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia.

In October, The New York Times reported Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia AI chips to Beijing, which are barred from shipment to China.

US officials reportedly concluded Ms Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and developed a close relationship with Mr Huang.

An image shared by software company Net Thunder on LinkedIn in 2024, which it says shows Alice Huang sitting alongside Jensen Huang at an event in Taiwan. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

The NYT reported Mr Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago and did nothing.

Further reporting over the weekend said US officials had intelligence Ms Huang was working for China's Ministry of State Security.

The Financial Times also reported the development, saying a memo circulated among top policymakers shortly before Mr Trump flew to Beijing for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this year.

The Chinese government dismissed the NYT report as "groundless speculation".

Who is Jensen Huang?

Mr Huang is an influential ally of Mr Trump and a leading figure in the US's efforts to dominate the AI race against China.

Mr Huang co-founded California-based Nvidia in 1993 and has served as president and chief executive ever since.

Leading AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI rely on Nvidia's hardware to operate, so the company wields a lot of power in the US and across the industry.

Who is Jensen Huang, the AI boss Trump calls at night? The founder of the world's most valuable AI company has the ear of Donald Trump when it comes to the risks and potential of the cutting-edge technology.

Nvidia surpassed Microsoft in June 2025 to become the world's most valuable company. A recent Forbes report said the company hit a market capitalisation of more than $US5 trillion ($7 trillion).

Mr Huang previously lobbied Mr Trump to lift a ban on the sale of advanced AI chips to China, arguing the restrictions accelerate Beijing's own development of the technology.

Mr Huang was born in Taiwan and raised in Thailand before he emigrated alone to the US to attend boarding school at 10 years old.

He met his wife, Lori, at university and the pair have been married for over 40 years.

Jensen Huang, with his wife Lori Huang, speaking to Tim Cook during a state dinner for Xi Jinping in September. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/AFP)

What do we know about the investigation?

Nvidia announced on Sunday, local time, it had launched an independent probe "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

It said while the company's board had "no reason to believe" either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the probe would "examine all available information".

Nvidia said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, would oversee the investigation.

Mr Huang will remain chief executive during the inquiry.

"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement.

" Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption. "

It is unclear if the CIA is also investigating.

The White House and CIA declined to comment to both the NYT and FT. Ms Huang could not be reached for comment by either outlet.

What has Huang said?

Shortly before Nvidia announced the probe, Mr Huang admitted to his affair with Ms Huang in a lengthy memo to staff.

He said he was "unfaithful" to his wife and there was "no excuse" for his actions, adding he was "deeply sorry".

Addressing the "national security concerns raised in news reports", he said he would fully cooperate with the investigation.

He said he was "committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security".

Jensen Huang's memo to staff Read more Read more I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. Jensen Huang Source: Bloomberg

How did Trump respond?

After Nvidia announced its investigation, Mr Trump said he had not spoken to Mr Huang about the allegations but said he had "done an amazing job for our country".

"I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on," Mr Trump told reporters.

Donald Trump reportedly was briefed a year ago about Jensen Huang's relationship to Alice Huang and her ties to Chinese intelligence. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

" I think he's an honourable guy … I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it. "

When asked if he would take Mr Huang on his trip to Asia next week, Mr Trump said: "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not comment on the matter.

"I just can't comment because of the nature of it," he told reporters on his way to a G7 meeting in Paris.

"And I also can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia."

What could come next?

Top Republicans in the US House of Representatives have called on Mr Huang to brief Congress this month about the reports.

Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat who will chair the Senate's foreign relations committee from January, shared the NYT report on social media with a pledge to open an investigation.

"The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," he said.

" Congress will investigate and get answers. "

Bloomberg's North Asia correspondent Minmin Low said there was uncertainty about what could come next.

"Will there be stricter restrictions when it comes to US investment overseas? Does this delay Nvidia's billions of dollars that are being poured into areas like advanced packaging and to its suppliers in Asia?" she told ABC's News Channel.

"If you look at the market reaction today, it seems like markets are quite resilient … investors are not seeing this as a change to the fundamentals of the AI trade.

"Of course, there is some short–term sentiment that is shaken at the moment, but a lot really rests on the ongoing investigation."

title: Looking for new fillings for sandwiches and wraps? We have you covered
text:
As we farewell soup and stew weather, we welcome perfect conditions for sandwiches and wraps.

These creative and versatile options could be served up at almost any time of day, and there's no need to spend hours babysitting a simmering pot.

In fact, most of these recipes involve minimal (if any) cooking time and many can be prepared (or partially prepared) ahead well before hunger strikes.

Have a batch ready to toast in a sandwich press as you need them, Lina Jebeile says. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

Lina Jebeile loves prepping these omelette breakfast sandwiches for suhoor (the pre-dawn meal during Ramadan) but says they are also a winner year-round.

Because they reheat beautifully in a sandwich press, they are a compelling contender for any busy mornings or office lunch.

Simple to make, easy to customise and perfect for prepping ahead.

Why confine this sanga strictly to mornings?

To make this layered roast vegetable sandwich vegan, simply omit the cheese. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon )

Hetty Lui McKinnon says this vegetable sandwich is perfect for picnics, but there's nothing stopping you from eating it inside too.

Inspired by one of America's iconic deli sandwiches, this vegetarian iteration of muffuletta uses roasted vegetables rather than cold cuts and the olive salad infuses every bite with a zesty punch.

This sandwich can also be made ahead. Just reach for some bread (focaccia or ciabatta recommended).

This recipe makes a chickpea filling for sandwiches or wraps, or for you to scoop up with crackers, Heidi Sze says. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Use this nourishing smash from Heidi Sze as you see fit, but between two slices of your preferred bread is an obvious (and delicious) choice.

This smash filling takes just 10 minutes and relies on a tin of inexpensive chickpeas as a base.

You can also play around with different flavour combinations, depending on your preferences and what you have handy. Trade parsley for chives, gherkins for capers or mayonnaise for plain yoghurt.

Loi Nguyen's version of traditional banh mi, a dish influenced by both French and Vietnamese cuisines. (ABC TV: Steve Brown)

Pickled carrots, mayonnaise and chilli sauce meets with thinly sliced marinated steak in this banh mi.

The time-consuming part is marinating the beef for 30 minutes beforehand, but fear not it only takes 3 to 5 minutes to cook it.

This take on a traditional crispy banh mi comes from Loi Nguyen, one of the accomplished home cooks taking part in the Recipe of the Year.

Marinating the chicken ahead of time takes the pressure off cooking at night. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Store-bought flatbreads, herby chicken, crunchy vegetables and a garlicky sauce are combined into an easy and satisfying meal in this recipe from Heidi Sze.

If weather and energy levels allow you could cook the chicken element of this meal on the barbecue, or even make the flatbread yourself.

title: Small businesses riding the 'personalisation' wave in retail
text:
When Mia Petterson was younger, her mum ran a retail store on Lonsdale Street in Braddon, in Canberra's inner north.

Fast forward to 2026, and Mia is following in her footsteps.

The 28-year-old curates vintage and second-hand items for her Blonde Concept store — which happens to be on the very same street her mum's was on.

"I just grew up around pretty things and clothes," she said.

Giving a personal touch to business is a priority for vintage and second-hand shop owner Mia Petterson. (ABC News)

"So the name, obviously not a huge amount of creativity involved in that, just got to be honest.

" But it's very true to me, and that's really what I wanted it to be. I wanted it to feel authentic and not forced. "

Since her mum's days working in the industry, Ms Petterson said retail had "100 per cent" changed, with buyers shifting towards secondhand and online purchasing.

Social media has become a huge part of the way people shop, too.

Loading Instagram content

Dr Andrew Hughes, a marketing lecturer at the Australian National University, said businesses who use social and digital platforms to boost and maintain engagement were more likely to succeed.

"Nowadays [shopping] combines the social factor as well," Dr Hughes said.

" Perhaps the person who runs the store is an influencer — that's so big nowadays in retail. You connect with a person who runs the store because you know them from social media, and then you visit their store second. "

'A case study in how to do marketing well'

Nationally, retail turnover is predicted to slow to 1.5 per cent next financial year, from 2.8 per cent, according to the latest quarterly forecast by Deloitte Access Economics.

But in the ACT, government data shows a near one per cent rise in the value of goods and services produced by the retail industry, indicating its increased value to the broader ACT economy.

Dr Hughes said retail results are often a "mixed bag", but successful businesses in the ACT that have managed to connect in multiple ways with their customers "are really a case study in how to do marketing well".

"They have good connection with their consumer base, they do good service provision and they're active on socials," he said.

Dr Andrew Hughes said the 'personalisation' of retail was impacting whether businesses sink or swim. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Ms Petterson said developing a relationship with her customers was "the only way to survive".

"I think one of my main priorities has always been creating a really comfortable, inviting environment for shoppers where they feel like they can try anything on, chat to me, like chat to the girls who work here, and I want people to leave feeling inspired," she said.

" Even if they don't leave with a piece of clothing, I want them to leave feeling excited to wear what they want and express themselves how they want. "

Mia Petterson followed after her own mum in running a retail store on Lonsdale Street, Braddon. (ABC News)

The 'personalisation' of industry

This personalised approach is something Dr Hughes believes will become a trademark of success in a new era of retail — and something that Australia's premier department store brand David Jones failed to adapt to.

"We're in a different environment," Dr Hughes said.

"People still spend, but the spending is linked in with experiences which are more personal to who they are.

" That personalisation effect, David Jones has not kept pace with. "

David Jones suppliers left with unpaid invoices David Jones's suppliers tell the ABC they could see "the writing on the wall" as payment times got longer and telephone calls went unanswered.

Dr Hughes said keeping up with younger markets was also key for retail businesses.

"For a lot of the younger markets, the most common thing I hear nowadays is, if I can't afford a [house], I'll spend some more money on retail," he said.

"Good for them, I get where they're at, you need some fun in life.

" If it isn't going to be eating noodles and toast and celebrating your first home, then why not have some fun spending that on some retail items. "

title: Leniu handed two-match ban after making money gesture to referees
text:
Parramatta's marquee off-season recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign — including the Eels' trip to Las Vegas — after being sin-binned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sin-binned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Against Samoa, Australia's old power conquered the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semifinal was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home-ground calls".

"It was a real home-ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home-ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

AAP

title: Luckless Test hopeful Morris continues horror injury run at party
text:
Test hopeful Lance Morris is again under an injury cloud after hurting his hand at a social event following Western Australia's one-day clash against England on Saturday.

It is understood Morris was at a party when he cut his non-bowling left hand.

Morris is set to consult a hand specialist today to determine the extent of the injury, and a timeline on his return to playing.

It comes just over a year after Morris had spinal fracture surgery he hoped would save his cricket career, after struggling to string games together in recent years.

Morris (centre) picked up three wickets in Western Australia's tour match against England at the weekend. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

There were encouraging signs in Saturday's outing as Morris finished with figures of 3–29 off 10 overs, claiming the wickets of England superstar Joe Root, as well as Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson.

Morris was called into Australia's Test squad in late 2022 after an impressive start to the Sheffield Shield season, with some considering it a matter of time until he made his Test debut.

However, since then he has managed just three one-day internationals, six Shield matches and 22 Big Bash games, due to a wretched injury run.

Ahead of last season Morris underwent stabilisation surgery, a process that involves bolts and wire being put into his lower back.

Labuschagne axed from Aussie squad for New Zealand Tests Australia's chairman of selectors confirms the omission of Marnus Labuschagne after an extended lean run of form at the Test level.

Just last week he told ABC Sport's Tom Wildie he hoped to bowl faster than ever after the procedure, hopeful it would not affect his pace and strength.

"That [a loss of pace] was a huge question for me leading into the surgery because I knew that was the asset that made me potentially selectable for red-ball cricket," he said last week.

"I had to look around at other guys that have had the surgery, the likes of Jofra [Archer], Jasprit Bumrah, the guys that have returned to Test cricket at the same speed if not better.

"I've got one eye on the speed gun at all times to see where things are at, but I'm pretty happy with where it's at."

With regular fast bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Captain Pat Cummins all well into their 30s, Australia is expected to soon be looking for other pace bowling options in the Test arena, with Morris long considered a likely contender for a spot in the XI.

title: 'Dedicated' apprentice jockey critical after race meet fall
text:
An apprentice jockey is fighting for her life after falling from a horse during a race in western NSW on the weekend.

Izzy Neale was riding in the Cotton Cup at Warren on Sunday when she suffered head injuries following a fall at the 400-metre mark during a 1,600m event.

The 22-year-old was treated onsite before being airlifted to Dubbo Hospital for further medical care, where she remains in a critical condition.

The horse she was riding, six-year-old Marnoo, suffered a near foreleg injury and was euthanased.

"The thoughts and heartfelt support of Racing NSW and the entire racing community are with Izzy, her family, friends and colleagues during this extremely difficult time," Racing NSW posted in a statement on X.

Fellow jockey Diego Montes de Oca was also dislodged from his horse, Shadow Dane.

He was transported to Dubbo hospital via road for injuries to his foot.

A Racing NSW spokesperson said Montes de Oca had since been discharged from hospital.

"Diego sustained soft tissue injuries to his left foot, with no fractures identified," the spokesperson said.

In a statement on social media, the Warren Jockey Club said its thoughts were with Izzy and her loved ones.

"The racing community is a close-knit one, and moments like these remind us just how much we stand together," the club said.

"We are all hoping for the very best for Izzy and are sending her strength, courage and our sincerest well wishes."

A 'dedicated' rider

Race caller Colin Hodges said the mood turned "very glum" after Neale was dislodged in front of the roughly 600 people in the crowd

The veteran caller of 57 years said he still remembered her first race at the Condobolin Picnic Races in 2024, where she pulled off an upset.

"She'd driven hundreds and hundreds of kilometres to western NSW," he said.

"[The horse] was probably the outsider of the whole race meeting."

Ms Neale won her debut race at Condobolin. (Supplied: Instagram )

Mr Hodges said Neale had assured her trainer at the Condobolin meet that she would ride well despite the odds.

"She certainly did because the horse was back running midfield and she just got into the perfect spot and won," he said.

Neale has had 88 wins out of 699 starts.

"She's become very, very successful," Mr Hodges said.

Race meeting postponed

In a statement on X, Racing NSW said it had postponed a meet in Scone today following consultation with jockeys and trainers that were set to take part.

"The decision follows the serious race fall involving apprentice jockey Izzy Neale at Warren yesterday," the statement said.

Racing NSW will be conducting an inquiry into the incident.

title: Alcaraz downs Shelton in final to claim maiden Paris Masters title
text:
Carlos Alcaraz says he feels proud of taking "one step forward mentally" after following up his Vienna title last week with a 7-6 (5), 7-5 victory over Ben Shelton in the Paris Masters final.

The Spanish showman, who missed more than four months of the season because of an injured right wrist, continued his late-season surge in style.

He has won all three finals he has reached since the US Open two months ago.

Alcaraz took his total to five titles for the year and 29 overall, including the Japan Open last month.

The second-seeded Alcaraz threw his arms out wide in celebration after clinching victory on his second match point with a two-handed backhand winner down the line at the indoor Plenitude Arena.

The seven-time grand slam champion cracked a broad smile and briefly appeared to cry after earning a ninth Masters title and first in Paris.

"It is something I have been chasing for a long time. Some of the toughest defeats I ever had in my career I have had here," Alcaraz said.

"Finally, I got my level here. I found the right path and the right way to do things."

With the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin starting next Sunday he feels in a good position to win that trophy for the first time, too.

"I would say this week I made one step forward mentally," Alcaraz said.

"Trying to be positive, trying to stay strong mentally. I'm happy I controlled my emotions every single match."

Earlier finish this time

Alcaraz won for the fourth time in five meetings with Shelton, who had beaten Alcaraz in a quarterfinal marathon at the US Open ending at 3:33am.

Shelton went on to reach the final, where he lost to Alexander Zverev.

There was to be no late marathon finish between Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton this time around. (Getty Images: Ibrahim Ezzat/NurPhoto)

Alcaraz saved six break points in the first set of Monday morning's final and overcame a break of serve in the second set by breaking the third-seeded Shelton straight back, no mean feat considering Shelton had 12 aces compared to six for Alcaraz.

"He is always in a position to attack after that serve," Alcaraz said.

"It is really difficult to dominate that ball. It is not only coming fast, it is coming with a lot of power."

Alcaraz, 23, did not drop a set in Vienna. But it was harder work in Paris and he almost went out on Friday, saving two match points against Taylor Fritz in their quarterfinal.

Shelton, 24, was seeking his eighth title overall and third Masters, having twice won the Montreal title.

The American recently added Juan Carlos Ferrero to his coaching staff, following on from Alcaraz's split with long-time coach Ferrero last year.

There is clearly no animosity between the players over that. Both congratulated each other's shots, and Alcaraz made a point of walking around the net to hug Shelton and pat him on the chest after winning.

Net battle

Both blessed with speed and agility, Alcaraz and Shelton drew each other to the net throughout, trading low, angled volleys.

Ben Shelton says he learns a lot from playing in big matches against the best. (Getty Images: Sport News/Quality Sport Images)

Pushing the other to the extremities of the court, there were some improbable retrieves, including one by Shelton in the ninth game when the American almost did the splits.

Shelton had an early advantage when he had Alcaraz 0-40 down in the fourth game. The Spaniard went on to save four break points before finally holding.

In the second set, Alcaraz was 4-2 down but broke Shelton back when he hit a forehand long from the back of the court.

After that he definitively changed the momentum.

Closing the gap

Shelton was "frustrated" at the missed opportunities, especially against someone like Alcaraz.

"The window is small. If you miss your chance, it's likely that another isn't going to come," he said. "It also speaks to his level, his ability to be clutch."

That is the next step for Shelton, who believes this defeat and the US Open final loss to Zverev will serve him well.

"When you get to play against the best consistently in big matches, I think that you learn so much," he said.

"Now going to Turin against the eight best players in the world, that's the positions that I want to be in."

title: Coach Aloisi oversees stunning capitulation in Chinese Super League title race
text:
John Aloisi's hopes of beginning his new coaching adventure with a title have spectacularly failed after the former Western United mentor's side capitulated on the final matchday.

The Socceroos legend was looking to become the next Australian to guide a team in China's top league to a championship after Kevin Muscat led Shanghai Port to glory in 2024 and 2025.

Aloisi's Chengdu Rongcheng were in the box seat to do so, leading the competition by 14 points with five rounds remaining and needing to pick up just one point to secure a maiden title.

The Sichuan club had also been top of the standings since the opening day, but things began to unravel when they lost three consecutive games while their main chasers, Dalian Yingbo, recorded three successive victories.

Going into the final matchday on Sunday, Dalian began three points behind Chengdu and defeated Tianjin Jinmen Tigers 3-1 in front of 60,000 fans.

Aloisi's club still only needed a point, but by 63 minutes in, they were 3-1 down to their final opponents Shandong Taishan.

Brazilian forward Wellington Silva did pull one back for Chengdu but they couldn't find the all-important equaliser, and Dalian claimed the title.

While Chengdu had a superior goal difference, the Chinese Super League prioritises head-to-head records between teams level on points and Dalian had won both meetings between them.

Footage showed furious fans yelling at Aloisi and his players at the team hotel following the match, with police stepping in to push the angry supporters back.

"We are indeed very disappointed not to have won the championship. We are in a very despairing state. There is nothing else to say," Aloisi told local media via a Chinese translator.

"I want to say sorry to everyone. We certainly know that our fans have travelled a long way to fight alongside us and support us.

"Right now, my only feeling is one of great dejection and disappointment, because we could see the trophy right in front of us, but could not get it."

Aloisi came to the Chinese Super League in January hoping to replicate the success he found with Western United in the A-League.

He led his team to the competition's championship in the 2021/2022 season, but his coaching career was thrown into limbo when the Melbourne-based club was placed into "hibernation" following legal issues and financial collapse last year.

He brushed away questions about whether he would resign because of the failure to secure the title in China.

"Now is not the time to talk about this," Aloisi said.

"As a team, together with the club and everyone, we need to review where we fell short in our past five matches. We need to face our problems, and then work on those aspects."

title: New Spirit ferries not using autopilot near Geelong after steering faults
text:
The operator of the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries has suspended autopilot use during transits of Port Phillip Bay as it probes the ships' steering faults.

Spirit IV was on its fifth-ever passenger voyage last Thursday when its primary steering system failed as it neared the bay en route to Geelong.

The issue occurred when the steering control was switched from autopilot to manual mode.

A back-up steering system ended up being used, and a tugboat was called to escort the ferry to Geelong, delaying its scheduled arrival by about four hours.

A track map shows Spirit IV made several turns outside Point Lonsdale before entering Port Phillip Bay. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

The incident came after a separate steering fault caused its sister ship, Spirit V, to briefly move outside the bay's charted shipping lane during a trial voyage in October.

Loading...

Both matters are now under investigation by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau.

On Monday, TT-Line chairman Ken Kanofski said last week's incident on Spirit IV involved a "frustratingly minor issue".

"There's an ongoing investigation, and I don't want to prejudice that by kind of declaring exactly that everything's been dealt with," Mr Kanofski told 936 ABC Hobart.

"When Spirit IV docked in Geelong, an inspection found a frustratingly minor issue with mechanical electrical processes in the steering console itself.

" And that was rectified and so the ship left that evening without incident. "

Ken Kanofski, pictured in May, says the steering issue on Spirit IV was caused by a "frustratingly minor issue". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Kanofski said the autopilot, which allows a ship to automatically follow a pre-determined route, is no longer being used when approaching and departing Geelong.

"So at the moment, we're not using autopilot in the bay, in Geelong, in Port Phillip Bay," Mr Kanofski said.

However, the autopilot will still be used once the ship reaches the open waters of Bass Strait, he said.

Mr Kanofski said the autopilot was never used for the ferries' arrival and departure at Devonport, in Tasmania's north-west.

"It's a very different entry to port than Geelong," he said.

"Obviously in Geelong you come in through the heads, and you've got quite a long way to navigate to get to port.

"In Devonport it's a very short distance, and so that's always been a completely manual process.

"But we've taken a range of interim measures to ensure that the ships and the passengers are safe, and that's our number one priority here."

The new Spirit of Tasmania ferries began carrying passengers across Bass Strait in late October. (Supplied: David Wallace)

The ABC asked TT-Line when it plans to resume its use of autopilot during transits of Port Phillip Bay.

A spokesperson said it had "no plans to resume the use of autopilot for all channel and close quarter navigation."

They said the situation would be reviewed once the ATSB releases its report, which is due by the middle of next year.

On Sunday, Spirit IV conducted an exercise off Devonport that was described by TT-Line as a "planned, routine check of its equipment".

title: Arena 'electric' as 36ers debutant hits buzzer beater
text:
Adelaide 36ers have had an epic three-year run with 46 consecutive sellout games, but few crowds have been louder than on Saturday night when 16-year old Raheim "RJ" Brown Jr hit a buzzer-beating three-pointer on debut.

"It was a crazy moment to hit the shot," Brown Jr told ABC Sport.

" It was electric in the arena. My ears were ringing after. The fans were crazy. "

The 36ers stormed to a 28-point win over Illawarra in the NBL match at the Adelaide Entertainment Centre on Saturday.

The point guard, who turned 16 a week ago, had been on the court for just 73 seconds when he made the shot.

The Year 10 student made headlines across the basketball world in September when the then-15-year-old became the youngest player signed by an NBL club in 44 years; and now sits behind John Horder and Craig Viney (who both played at 15 years and 8 months old) as the youngest debutants in history.

"It was totally a surprise. I was just waiting for my opportunity and when the coach put me in I tried to make the most of it," Brown Jr said.

Sitting in the crowd of over 10,000 were RJ's parents Coco and Raheim Brown Senior, who were elated when their son was injected into the game.

"We've been to every game as a fan to support the team … we never knew when that time was going to happen but RJ was prepared for it," Brown Snr said.

"Once he got out there and hit the shot I was electrified like the whole of Adelaide was. It was a really proud moment."

Deonte Williams (left) celebrates after Raheim Brown Jr (right) shoots a three-point at the end of the game. (Getty Images)

Brown Jr is a product of the Adelaide 36ers High Performance Schools Program that works across numerous metropolitan schools including Woodville High.

His talent transitioned into the NBL1 where he averaged 20 points per game in the West Adelaide senior reserves side and was able to feature nine times for the Bearcats.

Now in the NBL, he is training and learning alongside six-time MVP Bryce Cotton and five-time championship coach Trevor Gleeson.

"Pre-game warm ups, going through plays, they're all super locked in. They all take care of their body," Brown Jr said.

"The biggest thing is the pace of the game. It's a lot faster than NBL1, or under-18s."

The 36ers will be hoping Saturday's win is the catalyst to boost their chances this season.

Sitting fifth with a record of 6-6 they'll likely regain injured winger Flynn Cameron for Thursday night's clash with Melbourne United; and unveil new recruit Bul Kuol in December.

title: Labuschagne axed from Aussie squad for New Zealand Tests
text:
Marnus Labuschagne has been axed from Australia's Test squad.

Chairman of selectors George Bailey confirmed on Monday that Labuschagne would be omitted from Australia's yet-to-be-named squad for the first Test against New Zealand.

Australia's next Test begins on December 9 in Perth, but Bailey and his panel have made an early call to put Labuschagne out of his misery.

Bailey told reporters the out-of-form star wouldn't be considered for the entire four-Test series against New Zealand.

"This gives him a little bit of space and clears up a bit of conjecture … and we'll pick the rest of that squad at the end of round four of Sheffield Shield," Bailey said.

But a tortured tour of South Africa, where he logged scores of zero, four, 14, 39, 37 and 37, extended a miserable run of 49 innings without a Test century.

Labuschagne was briefly dropped for last year's tour of the West Indies, but batted his way straight back into the side for the home Ashes with two centuries for Queensland in the Sheffield Shield.

The 32-year-old, once touted as a future national captain by some pundits, will return to leading Queensland in the Shield as he bids to restore confidence and form.

title: Trump says he was 'kidding' about offering Dana White press secretary job
text:
US President Donald Trump has backtracked on his offer of the vacant White House press secretary role to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White, saying he was "only kidding".

Speaking to reporters before boarding Air Force One in Florida on Sunday evening, local time, Mr Trump said he still expected to speak with Mr White on Monday.

US President Donald Trump has backtracked on his White House press secretary job offer to UFC boss Dana White. (Reuters: Eric Lee)

Mr Trump also said he believed Mr White "loves the idea" of the job offer.

In his initial Truth Social post on Saturday, local time, Mr Trump described Mr White as "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and said he could appoint several well-known UFC stars as his assistants.

Donald Trump's original Truth Social post in which he announced the offering of a White House posting to Dana White. (Supplied: Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump)

On the tarmac in Florida a day later, the president said the nature of the post was a sign it was a joke.

He then told reporters that he was kidding five consecutive times in the same address.

Dana White has become a long-time ally of Donald Trump, who is known to frequently attend UFC championship bouts across the US. (Reuters: Supplied/Amber Searls/Imagn Images)

"If you saw the assistants, I posted the greatest wrestlers and UFC fighters in the world, right? Like Khabib, like Justin Gaethje who's phenomenal … You would've thought that people would've said, 'He's having a good time,'" Mr Trump said.

"I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea and there's only one Dana … It was just a little fun.

Loading...

"This was an example of something where I was kidding."

Of the six current or former UFC titleholders Mr Trump named in his post, two were athletes from ‌Russia's Dagestan region: Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov.

After Mr Trump's Truth Social post, Mr White posted his own image that appeared to show him standing at a White House lectern in the press briefing room, with a caption that read: "On to the next chapter."

The reaction image posted on social media by Dana White. (Supplied: Dana White)

The pair have forged a close working relationship over more than 20 years since the early 2000s, when Mr Trump's Taj ‌Mahal casino hosted UFC events.

Mr White has also previously spoken at Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and co-hosted the UFC Freedom 250 event on the South Lawn of the White House with Mr Trump in June.

Before to Mr Trump's comments in Florida, Politico's White House correspondent Daniel Lippman told ABC NewsRadio he did not believe in the legitimacy of the job offer.

"Usually Trump, when he puts something on social media, he doesn't really joke around that much, he doesn't have a big joke gene … I'm putting my money that this is not real and Trump is just trying to troll and stay in the media," he said.

Mr Lippman said Mr White, who has an estimated net worth of more than $US600 million according to Forbes, would need to take "a big pay cut" to enter the Trump administration.

He also questioned whether Mr White would have the political experience and knowledge necessary to be a successful White House staffer.

"Trump does want a fighter for his next press secretary, especially as Democrats control Capitol Hill and they will be hounding him," he said.

"Maybe [Mr White] just wouldn't have press briefings and he would just be more of a symbolic head of the White House press office."

The White House press secretary posting has remained vacant for close to a month after Katie Zacharia left the position less than a week into the role.

Mr Trump's post about Mr White came a day after he announced that his chief of staff Susie Wiles would be replaced by her hardline deputy Stephen Miller.

On Sunday, local time, CBS News reported that a day after his appointment, Mr Miller revealed Richard Walters — a known ally of Ms Wiles who had replaced Mr Miller as deputy chief of staff — would be leaving the role.

"While he will be leaving us, Richard will continue to help from the outside as we continue to work with all of our strength to deliver for President Trump and his courageous fight to save America," Mr Miller said, according to CBS News.

The series of White House appointment changes comes days after the Trump administration and Republican Party suffered deep losses in nationwide midterm elections.

The GOP lost control of the House of Representatives and the Senate to the Democrats.

Almost half-a-million Brisbane residents could receive scheduled respite from aircraft noise under a new package of flightpath changes released for public consultation, but Airservices Australia has discarded two other options its own consultants found were technically viable. Airservices announced five options for community consultation on Monday as part of the final package of the Noise Action Plan for Brisbane Airport, saying the proposals could provide periods of respite from aircraft arrivals for about 482,000 residents – and reduce aircraft noise for a further 139,000 – through higher altitudes and smoother descents. Airservices Australia is exploring ways to lesson the impact of aircraft noise from Brisbane Airport operations. Brisbane Airport “The options we are presenting provide a real opportunity for noise improvements for some of the communities we have most frequently engaged with throughout the Noise Action Plan for Brisbane,” Airservices Australia program delivery head Donna Marshall said. “New runway-aligned communities, who are subject to both arrival and departure operations, could receive respite from arrivals in between peak traffic periods on an alternating basis with legacy runway communities.

Advertisement

“Communities to the north and west of the airport, who are overflown by aircraft arriving to the new runway, could also experience lower noise levels from the increased flightpath altitudes and smoother descent profiles. Some of these communities could also benefit from respite options.” The options emerged from a detailed review by aviation consultancy Trax International, which examined Brisbane’s complex airspace system and assessed 17 concepts aimed at reducing the impact of aircraft noise on surrounding communities. Related Article Perspective

Brisbane Airport Is a noisy sky simply the price you pay for living in a thriving city? But while the Trax report identified seven concepts as viable for further consideration, Airservices ultimately narrowed that list to five, despite the remaining two concepts being found technically feasible. The five options out for public consultation include two noise-sharing runway operation concepts and three arrival flightpath changes designed to keep aircraft higher over residential areas for longer.

Advertisement

One proposal would give some Brisbane suburbs regular breaks from aircraft arriving overhead. On days when winds came from the north, planes would be directed to just one runway for arrivals, giving those under the other runway’s flightpaths respite. Airservices estimated the arrangement could be used on about 100 weekdays a year when traffic and weather conditions allowed. Related Article Brisbane Airport Airport noise costs Brisbane $100m a year, curfew would cost $10m, report claims A second proposal would extend those respite periods by allowing more departing aircraft to use over-water runway ends, potentially delaying the need to return to normal runway operations. The remaining proposals focus on making aircraft quieter by keeping them higher above suburbs as they approach Brisbane Airport. One would allow planes arriving from the south and east at night to remain hundreds of metres higher over existing flight paths, benefiting about 50,000 residents. Another would do the same for nighttime arrivals from the north and west, while a third would permanently raise aircraft altitudes on several arrival routes from the north and west during both day and night operations. Aircraft would also spend less time flying level over populated areas, reducing noise on the ground.

Advertisement

But the most contentious finding in the report may be what has not been put before the public. Trax found viable a broader noise-sharing concept, known as Concept 10, that would have provided predictable respite in both northerly and southerly wind conditions by alternating all four of Brisbane Airport’s segregated runway modes. The report found it would offer the most comprehensive respite arrangement and could operate regardless of wind direction. Airservices rejected the proposal after concluding the new departure routes required to make it work would newly affect about 136,000 residents, including people in Coorparoo, Holland Park, Salisbury, Macgregor, Parkinson, Browns Plains, Regents Park and Boronia Heights. South-east Queensland’s congested airspace. Airservices Australia The report estimated about 198,700 people would be exposed to aircraft noise events above 60 decibels beneath one proposed new route, compared with about 41,700 beneath the existing path.

Advertisement

Another proposal would have diverted some non-jet aircraft onto a new approach path from the north. Airservices rejected the idea, finding it would affect about 70,000 residents while delivering benefits for only a handful of flights. Trax found there was “little uncommitted airspace” in south-east Queensland, with Brisbane operations constrained by Defence airspace around Amberley and offshore training areas, airports at the Gold and Sunshine coasts, general aviation operations at Archerfield and existing air traffic control systems. Trax examined seven broader airspace redesign concepts, including rerouting departures over Moreton Bay, using Amberley airspace for civil arrivals and relocating Sunshine Coast traffic to improve Brisbane operations. None were considered viable. Public consultation on the five shortlisted options will run until December 13, after which Airservices planned to determine whether any proposals should proceed. TMK Energy has notched up a double win at its wholly-owned Gurvantes XXXV coal seam gas project in Mongolia, smashing another monthly production record and securing regulatory acceptance of its declaration of (gas) discovery, putting it firmly on the path to a potential 30-year production licence. The dual achievements come as the company kicks off a new drilling and well enhancement campaign designed to push the project towards commerciality. The company says average daily gas production for October jumped 11 per cent to 971 cubic metres per day (m³/day), up from 872m³/day in September. TMK Energy prepares for well re-completions at its recently declared Lucky Fox gas discovery within the Gurvantes XXXV project in Mongolia. The October record of 34,300 standard cubic feet per day came without any contribution from new wells, with field uptime remaining high despite brief power cuts and water production holding steady at 410 barrels daily. At the seven-well Lucky Fox pilot in the Nariin Sukhait coal district, TMK is pumping water from the coal seams to lower reservoir pressure and coax trapped methane into flowing, a process known as “desorption”. Spanning 8400 square kilometres of Mongolia’s South Gobi Basin, Gurvantes XXXV boasts an independently certified 2C contingent resource of 1.2 trillion cubic feet of gas (Tcf) already discovered but not yet commercially developed. Another 5.3Tcf of prospective resources adds serious exploration upside. A drilling rig and workover rig are now on site, giving TMK the firepower to kick its gas ambitions up another gear. And rather than splash out on a swag of new wells, the company is looking to squeeze more gas from its existing producers through a lower-cost re-completion program. TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson said: “With the 2026 Work Program now underway, we expect to see further significant increases in gas production rates over the next few months as both LF-08 is brought into production and the three well re-completions are undertaken.” Following equipment-delivery delays, the campaign kicked off in October with the cleanout of idle well LF-03, setting the stage for the first of three planned re-completions. If the current re-completions deliver the goods, the technique could be rolled out across the remaining Lucky Fox wells, giving TMK another cost-effective lever to lift gas flows. Adding to the project’s credentials, the company is pushing ahead with a proposed one-megawatt gas-to-power plant at site alongside local partner Dashvaanjil Group, with engineering and costings complete. A final investment decision has shifted to the first quarter of 2027, allowing fresh production data to guide engine sizing and help avoid excess flaring. The plant could power TMK’s operations and nearby industrial customers. The bigger prize could lie just across the border in China. Coal supplies 85 per cent of Mongolia’s primary energy. Dalaroo Metals has delivered another significant gold intersection at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire, West Africa, hitting a 13-metre-thick zone of mineralisation grading 2.67 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 87m depth. The interval, at its fresh Wilfred prospect, also included a higher-grade six-metre core running at 4.19g/t gold from 87m and is just 1.25 kilometres along strike from its recent high-grade Fournier discovery. Other intercepts in the same hole include 7m going 0.84g/t gold from 63m, 6m assaying 0.78g/t gold from 78m and a deep single-metre interval grading 16.2g/t from 187m. Dalaroo Metals’ diamond drill pad set up ready for follow-up drilling at its high-grade West African Fournier gold discovery. The latest headline hit at the Wilfred prospect confirms that the company’s spectacular maiden discovery hole at Fournier last month was no flash in the pan. The Fournier discovery comprises results from two opposing holes drilled to more than 200m depth as part of Dalaroo’s maiden reverse circulation (RC) drilling orientation program at the project. The scissored holes were the first drilling undertaken across the seven-kilometre-long Gold Ridge target corridor. One of those two holes returned a headline hit of 18m at 7.31g/t gold from 63m and a second, deeper zone of 16m at 1.46g/t gold from 113m. The opposing hole, collared 43m northeast of the headline hole, also gave up a healthy 23-metre intercept assaying 2.14g/t gold from surface.

’What is particularly encouraging is the occurrence of significant gold mineralisation at widely separated locations.” Dalaroo Metals managing director John Morgan Now, with a similar style of mineralisation appearing 1.25km away on the northernmost Wilfred section - directly along strike from Fournier - Dalaroo believes it could be on the cusp of defining a potentially significant mineralised corridor. For explorers, geological consistency is a major tick in the box when working to prove up a large-scale, economic deposit. It suggests a predictable and potentially extensive system. Dalaroo says that while its results so far show meaningful gold grades and widths at the two widely separated locations, mineralisation continuity between sections has not yet been established. However, Dalaroo says the similarity of alteration, quartz-sulphide veining and prospective host rocks at the two locations supports its working model of a possibly uniform and major structurally controlled gold system. Dalaroo Metals managing director John Morgan said: “The intersection of a new zone of significant gold mineralisation at the Wilfred Prospect, 1.25km from the Fournier discovery hole, is an excellent result and strongly supports our view that a large mineralised system is present at Bondoukou. We are very encouraged by the fact that the results from the first two prospects drilled at the Bondoukou Gold Ridge have both delivered significant gold intercepts from our maiden drilling program.”

Encouraged by the latest results and with growing promise of potentially bigger things ahead, the company says it’s moving immediately to crank up an expanded 1750-metre diamond drilling program, alongside preparations for a major induced polarisation (IP) geophysical survey. The Wilfred and Fournier prospects are both situated on the 40-kilometre-long Bondoukou Gold Ridge, a major regional structure which has seen little modern exploration. Dalaroo’s early maiden drilling successes suggest the entire ridge could be highly prospective for further gold discoveries. With its apparently persistent, open-ended mineralisation along strike and at depth, the Wilfred area offers an abundance of immediate follow-up drill targets. That 1.25-kilometre-long stretch of untested ground between Fournier and Wilfred now looms as a high-priority target zone for Dalaroo. Any success in connecting the two prospects could quickly elevate the scale of the company’s find. Dalaroo’s maiden drilling program at Bondoukou represents the first ever drilling put into the ground and it has already thrown up two significant gold discoveries at two separate but potentially structurally-linked prospects, returning significant gold intercepts in eight of the twelve holes reported to date. The company appears well-funded to accelerate its exploration plans, reporting a cash position of $3.1 million at the end of the recent October quarter.

Singapore Airlines’ overhaul of its business class seats has triggered a social media backlash from potential travellers who are taking aim at the “progressive” look for not being in sync with the iconic brand. Sporty like jeans and sneaker. The new Singapore Airlines business class seat. Chris Zappone While the seating itself appears slick and functional, the new colour scheme is drawing significant criticism across social media, with one user posting: “Last chance to fly Singapore Airlines before they make it ugly.” In a jab to the global design group commissioned to upgrade the airline’s business livery, another said: “It’s really European and does not align with Singapore values.” Another claimed: “A Singaporean designer would’ve done much better.”

Julia de Bono, the CEO from BMW Designworks, the company hired by Singapore Airlines to design the seat, said “the palate was deliberate”. She said the “warmer” look had “served the airline for a long time, and many of the cabins are going warm and more traditional right now”. “But we wanted this business class to stand on its own, with its own attitude modern, progressive, and refreshing.” US-based De Bono told an audience of journalists that: “We wanted the cabin to feel high-tech, luxurious, and future-forward. Mineral greys – you see them everywhere right now – they are really having this balance and stable feel to them.”

The new Singapore Airlines business class seat. Chris Zappone In the refresh, the premium economy seats are a warm grey-blue, with orange accents, while economy seats are blue with grey trim. “The new design doesn’t elevate the brand look… it makes Singapore Airlines look like they are having an identity crisis,” she said. There is also an undercurrent of national identity for an airline that is closely associated with the nation. One Singapore-based commenter wrote: “If you get a non-Singaporean who [does] not live the culture, the essence[,] and appreciate the legacy of [Singapore Airlines] this is what you get. International Rugby League chairman Troy Grant has defended the decision to permit players to represent the nation where one of their great-grandparents were born, as Samoa forward Spencer Leniu lashed out at World Cup organisers, claiming “they’ve used our people to sell games”. The new eligibility rules were announced in Sydney on Monday as the Pacific and the United States were confirmed as the host of the next World Cup in 2030. Loading Leniu said holding the next edition in the region “shows the importance of our people in growing our game”, but took a shot at the huge gulf in player payments at this World Cup as he was hit with a grade-three charge over an incident that led him to be sin-binned during Samoa’s 44-12 semi-final defeat to Australia on Sunday night. “Let’s be honest, our little nations carried this WC. Yet we are paid $850 a game [compared] to the Aussies [who get] 30/40k for the tournament,” Leniu wrote in a social media post.

He is facing a two-game suspension, which would rule him out of Parramatta’s NRL opener in Las Vegas next season, after being hit with a contrary conduct charge for making a gesture towards referee Adam Gee. The incoming Parramatta enforcer said it was “no secret that they’ve used our people to sell games” and believes they should be properly rewarded for it. Samoan supporters make their presence felt during Sunday night’s World Cup semi-final against Australia at Allianz Stadium. Getty Images Members of the Australian team receive $40,000 each for the World Cup under the Rugby League Players’ Association’s collective bargaining agreement with the Australian Rugby League Commission, while players from other countries have received $850. “Taking the next WC to the US, specifically Utah and Hawaii, where there is a big Polynesian community shows the importance of our people in growing our game,” Leniu said. “So I believe if they are going to use that as a tool to generate money, our little nations should be compensated fairly for it.”

The ARL Commission will organise and run the 2030 tournament, which will be staged in a Magic Round-style format with a full slate of men’s and women’s pool matches to be played over three days in one stadium before moving onto another venue. Under the format, the group stage will take place at up to five venues from Australia to the US, with potential host cities and states including Sydney, Brisbane, Auckland, Hawaii and Utah. Spencer Leniu is facing a two match ban for making a gesture towards referee Adam Gee. While payers have previously been allowed to wear the colours of a country where one of their parents or grandparents was born, they can now point to the nation of birth of one of their eight great-grandparents.

Advertisement

Sport governing bodies such as World Rugby, FIFA and World Athletics also have a grandparent rule. But the IRL’s extension to another generation in a player’s lineage puts the code in a league of its own. Raiders fullback Kaeo Weekes will be able to represent the Cook Islands under new eligibility rules. Getty Images “It may not be as pure as some people may think it should be, or fit their mindsets. I don’t really care about that,” said Grant, a former NSW racing minister. “I care about growing the game and giving every player the opportunity to represent their nation and I care that the fans are getting the best outcomes, which we have seen during this World Cup.”

International rugby league has enjoyed the fruits of players embracing their heritage, particularly those from Pacific Island backgrounds. Tonga and Samoa, who met in an unforgettable pool game at CommBank Stadium eight days ago, have become heavyweights as a result. The new move is a shameless bid to spread even more NRL talent around the globe, no matter how distant the connection between players and the nation of their forebears. Luke Keary in action for Ireland at the 2022 World Cup. He qualified for the country via his paternal grandfather. Getty Images Grant cited Canberra fullback Kaeo Weekes as a player who could benefit from the updated rules, saying they would have allowed him to turn out for the Cook Islands at this World Cup if they had been in place before the tournament. “I think we have players sitting on the sidelines who the public deserve to see show their skills,” Grant said.

“We want the best players available and with the economic conditions, the way the geopolitical world’s operating, there is a lot of movement from nation to nation. Related Article Rugby League World Cup Walsh sinks Samoa as Kangaroos set up blockbuster World Cup final showdown with Kiwis “I think it enhances rather than in any way undermines the game into the future.” The call was made nine months after a State of Origin eligibility shake-up that freed New Zealand internationals to also play for NSW and Queensland, clearing the way for Maroons star Kalyn Ponga to declare his allegiance to the Kiwis. Grant said the IRL board had also committed to explore elevating Tonga and Samoa to tier-one nations.

“They’ve lit up international rugby league like we haven’t seen before and we’re enormously grateful for that,” he said. Despite the 2030 World Cup being hosted by the Pacific and the US, it’s highly unlikely that the group-stage travelling roadshow will reach the likes of Fiji, Tonga and Samoa due to limited infrastructure there such as stadiums and hotels. title: A suspected spy, a powerful CEO and a global contest: The Nvidia controversy explained
text:
IN BRIEF The CEO of one of the world's most important tech companies has confirmed he had an affair.

US intelligence agencies say the affair was with a Chinese spy who was sharing information.

One of the world's most powerful technology bosses is embroiled in an investigation over reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting concerns of a national security breach.

Jensen Huang, the boss of American AI chipmaking giant Nvidia, apologised for the affair in a company message, saying he had been unfaithful to his wife.

"There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

Nvidia said it would open an investigation into the reports Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" but has denied any breaches of company secrets or national security.

The company has become one of the most significant technology firms in the world, supplying the chips that AI companies need and fuelling the exponential rise of the sector. Its 2026 revenue topped US$216 billion ($311 billion) in the last financial year.

Who is the suspected spy?

United States media has named her as Alice Huang, a former TV reporter in China and more recently a top executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

That company is one of Nvidia's biggest clients in Southeast Asia. US authorities have been looking into Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.

The New York Times newspaper reported last month that US intelligence agencies determined the Chinese citizen had been feeding information to Beijing.

READ MORE Chinese AI app DeepSeek banned on all Australian government devices

It's unclear what that information was or how valuable it was.

Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment from US media.

What has Nvidia said about the affair?

Nvidia's board said in a statement its inquiry would examine all available information but that it had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised".

It said its CEO was cooperating with the investigation and will remain in the job during the inquiry.

Huang has already been called on by key Republican politicians to brief Congress this month about the US media reports.

The report raises "significant national security concerns regarding [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information", the Republicans said in a letter dated 4 November.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

Why is Nvidia so important?

The company is at the centre of a geopolitical contest between the US and China. Its products have become strategically important for both countries trying to outmanoeuvre the other.

China wants to establish its own chip-making industry and rely less on US products, including investing in domestic products from Huawei. It wants to set up a world-leading semiconductor industry by 2030.

The US has restricted exports of advanced chips to stem China's access to powerful AI technology, fearing its impact on weapons-making. Nvidia complies with those restrictions.

"US actions have also sought to sustain US leadership in advanced chips, related parts of the semiconductor supply chain, and computing and AI applications, while slowing China's development of competitive capabilities," a 2025 research report by foreign policy expert Karen M Sutter said.

"US actions have been grounded in concerns about PRC [People's Republic of China] efforts to build an indigenous, self-sufficient, and secure and controllable semiconductor ecosystem; and PRC military-civil fusion policies that seek to use commercial advancements in semiconductors, AI, and other technologies for military uses."

title: Why your next specialist visit could cost a lot more than expected
text:
IN BRIEF Fees to see specialist doctors have gone up by around 4 per cent in the past year.

One think tank says the share of fee-free care is falling and some fees are rising faster than inflation.

Calls are growing to penalise doctors for overcharging some of the two million Australians who pay 'extreme' fees to see specialists every year.

A new report by public policy think tank the Grattan Institute found specialist fees, including for services such as psychiatry, dermatology and paediatrics, continue to soar — some rising by almost 20 per cent in the past year.

It said 800,000 Australians a year are skipping or delaying specialist care because of cost.

Meanwhile, more than two million pay at least one extreme fee a year.

"This broken system needs an overhaul, including penalising specialists who routinely charge patients more than three times the Medicare schedule fee," the institute's report authors argued.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Which services are getting more expensive?

Across all specialist medical services, the average specialist fee has gone up by 4 per cent, on top of inflation, in the last year.

Seeing a dermatologist for the first time is now 7 per cent more expensive than a year ago. For psychiatry, it's now 20 per cent more expensive than last year, which means fees are going up by about $50 a year.

READ MORE More Australians are seeing a GP. What happens next is becoming more complex

Some specialists charge more than their peers — the most expensive 5 per cent of psychiatrists charge a median out-of-pocket fee of $669 for an initial consultation. For high-cost paediatricians, it is $362. For high-cost cardiologists, it is $265.

While some services receive a partial government subsidy through the Medicare Benefits Schedule, Grattan says patient fees have "skyrocketed", and the share of fee-free care is falling. It said some fees are rising faster than inflation.

Why are specialist fees so high?

Doctors' groups say they shouldn't be blamed for the soaring costs of providing specialist services.

The Australian Medical Association blames inadequate Medicare rebates, private health insurer benefits, case complexity, geography, and workforce supply for the out-of-pocket fees.

Grattan doubts doctors' claims that fees are rising because government funding hasn't kept up with the costs of providing care, or because of costs such as staff, equipment, insurance, and rent.

It said the "real problem" is an unrestrained market with no controls on fees, which it said has been left on "autopilot" for too long.

For example, it said government rebates rose by 8.7 per cent in the past three years, but were "dwarfed" by the 30.6 per cent rise in specialist fees over the same period.

While median costs per business grew by 30 per cent overall, profits grew 70 per cent.

"Patients rarely choose their specialist, cannot easily judge the quality of care, and often cannot find out the price they will pay until they have booked their appointment, or even until they get the bill," it said.

What can be done to tackle soaring fees?

Apart from regulating and reining in extreme fees, Grattan says the government could expand public clinics in areas with too little care, train more specialists, and give every GP easy access to specialist advice.

Grattan also wants to introduce an "annual rule" — where if a specialist's fees average more than triple the Medicare Benefits Schedule fee across a year, they would be required to pay back the Medicare rebates for their services that year.

This would affect fewer than 2,000 specialists — about 6 per cent.

"To make sure Australians can get the care they need, governments must fix those structural problems, not just spend more," it said.

title: Two Australians survive helicopter crash in Indonesia while fighting wildfires
text:
Two Australians pilots have survived their fire helicopter crashing in a river in Indonesia on Sunday.

Rescuers are searching for a third crew member, an Indonesian citizen, after the aircraft fell into the Barito River in South Kalimantan province, according to the country's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB).

The two Australians were receiving medical treatment, the BNPB said.

An 18-member rescue team was sent to search for the missing crew member.

The incident comes as Indonesia experiences its worst wildfires in a decade, with Australia deploying firefighting personnel to help battle the blazes.
