title: Major Australian employers are cutting jobs. What does it mean for the economy?
text:
In brief Australia's biggest employers have cut thousands of jobs in recent weeks.

Some predict this could impact the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision on interest rates.

Some of Australia's biggest employers are cutting thousands of jobs, and economists are asking whether the "resilient" job market is starting to crack — and is another sign of an impending recession.

From banking and mining to digital services — the job cuts have been mixed across various sectors.

Last week, the country's digital design giant, Canva, announced it will cut or relocate more than 1,200 jobs — 22 per cent of its workforce — in what was described as the company's first restructuring in 13 years.

Just a day later, gas giant Woodside Energy announced it would cut at least 500 jobs globally as part of a cost-cutting process, with 80 per cent of its workforce based in Australia.

On the same day, the country's iconic retailer David Jones announced it had entered voluntary administration.

The job-cutting trend has also hit the banking sector, with National Australia Bank (NAB) announcing plans to cut 2,500 jobs by the end of the financial year in October.

"They're significant. In some cases, some of these businesses are shedding," Robert Breunig, an Australian National University pubic policy economist, told SBS News.

"It's hundreds or even thousands of jobs, and it's a large fraction of their workforce.

"But in terms of the number of overall jobs in the economy, it's still just a relatively small piece of the picture."

What's leading the major job cuts?

These under-pressure employers face different disruptions.

Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said in a statement on the job cuts that "new technology is transforming what people can create" and "small changes won't be enough" — without directly naming artificial intelligence (AI).

David Jones's announcement came after years of mounting pressure on traditional department stores from changing shopping habits, online competition and expensive property decisions.

And NAB blamed challenging economic conditions, technological change, competition and a need to simplify its operating model.

Robert Brooks, a professor in the department of econometrics at Monash University, says each company announcement offers "different lessons" to be learnt.

"Canva is obviously a newer company at a much earlier stage, and it's working through what its appropriate business model is in a digital transformation setting," he told SBS News.

"David Jones is a mature company in a mature industry that's been significantly impacted by technological change and changing people's retail purchase patterns.

"The banking sector ones are somewhere in between. [They] are obviously a very mature and sophisticated economic sector. They're clearly in a business model that is being disrupted, but a lot of their business has a tremendous go-forward version."

A 'less resilient' job market

The job cuts have happened while Australia's unemployment rate climbed to 4.7 per cent in September — its highest level since October 2021, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

That figure, coupled with the company cuts, has raised questions about the strength of the job market.

"The [job] market has been really resilient up to a point. It's been able to absorb a lot of significant policy change, and it's been able to absorb a lot of geopolitical shocks," Brooks said.

"What we've seen in the more recent data is this picture where the market has become slightly less resilient.

He said although people should watch the current job market "incredibly carefully", there is not enough information to show that it has started to crack.

The ABS figure showed almost 40,000 people lost their jobs in September, while 732,000 people were unemployed nationwide.

Breunig said while Australia's job market is not doing as well as a year ago, the Australian economy remains pretty robust.

"We often talk about job losses because those are the things that get the media attention, but there are also thousands of jobs that are created every day. And Australia does have a very dynamic small business sector."

He warned that the rise in the unemployment rate might affect the country's economy as a whole.

"It does put the government in a difficult position because they're gonna have to pay more in income support payments to people. They're also gonna get less tax revenue from fewer workers," he said.

Is Australia headed for a recession?

More job losses are expected in the coming months following the Reserve Bank's rate hike in November from 4.6 per cent to 4.85 per cent — the highest since 2008.

Economists and social services groups are bracing for the unemployment rate to rise in the coming months, with higher interest rates generally leading to higher unemployment rates.

"The effect is that it makes people feel poorer because they're spending more money on their mortgage. So they have less money to spend in the economy ... and that ripples through to lower employment," Breunig said.

"And then, [in] the long term, AI is very likely to displace jobs. It will create other jobs, and other jobs will come along. But again, the kind of short- to medium-term effect of AI is also likely to push the unemployment rate up."

Persistently higher unemployment can affect the entire country's economy, potentially leading to a recession — something the RBA has said it wants to avoid.

One way of detecting the onset of a recession by measuring unemployment is the 'Sahm rule': it considers a recession is underway when the three-month average unemployment rate is at least 0.5 per cent higher than its lowest level in the past year. However, the RBA adjusts this to 0.75 per cent for Australia.

Here, the jobless rate averaged 4.63 per cent from July to September, up from 4.17 per cent between December and February — a 0.46-percentage-point increase that falls short of the Sahm rule threshold.

Last week, while announcing the fifth rate rise of the year, RBA governor Michele Bullock said that it will "make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer".

But she said the bank "is not looking to tip the economy into a recession if we can avoid it".

One factor that could influence a rate cut is rising unemployment.

The potential impact on employment was also among the factors the RBA's board considered at its last meeting, when six board members voted to raise rates, while three voted to leave them unchanged.

Brooks said part of the reason for the split vote was questions about whether the rate increase will have "a large spike in unemployment that the labour market can't quite deal with".

"I think from part of the commentary and the discussion that's come out from the recent decision, they are clearly going to need to take a look.

"More data that tells us that unemployment is continuing to rise would suggest that we wouldn't wanna push too hard further on contractionary monetary policy."

title: Donald Trump offers UFC chief Dana White job as White House press secretary
text:
In brief Donald Trump invited UFC chief Dana White to be the new White House press secretary in a social media post.

The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia's brief tenure ended last month.

United States President Donald Trump has asked mixed martial arts promoter Dana White to serve as White House press secretary and called on him to bring some fighters along as assistants "even though some are not from our country."

White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, is a "violent fighter and warrior", Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.

Trump also asked for six current or former UFC titleholders to join White, including two athletes from Russia's Dagestan region, Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov, Americans Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and "Kayla Harris," likely a reference to Kayla Harrison, and Amanda Nunes, a Brazilian native who became a US citizen last year.

"We need these people to defend us against the lunatic left," Trump wrote.

White and UFC's parent company, TKO Group Holdings, did not immediately return requests for comment. However, CNN reported White has declined the presidentsy's invitation.

The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia's tenure ended last month after less than a week. Zacharia replaced Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August.

White and Trump first worked together in the early 2000s, when Trump's Taj Mahal casino hosted some UFC events. But they have become closer allies since the UFC chief publicly backed Trump's presidential campaign in 2016.

In recent years, Trump has attended several UFC events, and in June the White House hosted a night of UFC fights as part of celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of US independence.

Post-election shake-up

Trump's invitation to White comes after the president named his trusted aide Stephen Miller as chief of staff, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller steps in as the Republican Party's defeat in Wednesday's midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors", and he praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job". Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

A White House official said Miller’s appointment signals that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.

title: How thousands of 'special votes' will now determine New Zealand's election winner
text:
IN BRIEF The NZ election has ended without a clear winner.

The result could be decided by 700,000 votes and minor party negotiations.

It could be weeks before the winner of New Zealand's general election emerges, with neither of the two major parties securing enough seats to form a government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party secured 42 seats in the country's parliament, while former Prime Minister Chris Hipkins' centre-left Labour Party won 36 seats.

The National Party, combined with its coalition partners ACT and NZ First, had a projected count of 67 seats, according to the NZ Electoral Commission.

Opposition parties Labour, the Greens and the Māori Party, together with the new force Opportunity — which has not yet said which side it will join in a coalition — combined for 63 seats.

Luxton has said that he is confident in securing another term, while Hipkins has said he will wait for the final results.

Final results in weeks

To control the New Zealand parliament, a party needs a majority of 61 seats out of the baseline 120 seats.

However, under New Zealand's Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) voting system, the total number of seats can increase because of "overhang seats", changing the number needed for a majority. Voters can decide how many seats a party gets during the election.

In the current election, the majority needed to lead is 66 seats, according to the country's public broadcaster, Radio New Zealand (RNZ).

READ MORE New Zealand election still on a knife edge with more than 90 per cent of votes counted

In the party vote, Labour had a narrow majority, with 29.36 per cent, while National secured 29.21 per cent, according to RNZ.

The Greens recorded their best-ever national vote, on 13.30 per cent, as did ACT, on 10.92 per cent, while NZ First was at 9.78 per cent and Opportunity at 5.96 per cent.

The results might also change when an estimated 700,000 'special votes' from out-of-electorate and overseas ballots — which typically favour the left — are added to the mix.

They will all be included on November 27, when the final results are released, meaning it might take weeks to understand who will be in charge of New Zealand's next government.

About 400,000 special votes remain to be counted, including 96,000 from overseas.

While the final results will be announced in weeks, the current New Zealand prime minister has said he is confident of a second term.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he's confident of another term in government while Labour leader Chris Hipkins says results are still being counted. Source: Getty, AAP / Hagen Hopkins / Ben McKay

'Time to sit tight'

Luxon said his National Party had secured the most seats, giving them a mandate to form government.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders have given us the biggest seats in parliament, 42 seats as it stands today and a pathway to form a government."

But he said his party and all New Zealanders now needed to wait for the final results on 27 November.

If he does secure another term, it could be without important figures in the election: finance minister Nicola Willis, defence minister Paul Goldsmith and speaker Gerry Brownlee, who all conceded their races, while transport minister Chris Bishop is also a likely loser.

"Some of the hardest phone calls tonight have been to colleagues and friends who look unlikely to make it back into parliament," Luxon said.

Meanwhile, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said on Saturday that he will wait for the final results.

"As things stand tonight, it's clear we're not going to know the exact shape of the next government for a little while longer yet," he said.

"When the final result is known, I'll have quite a bit more to say."

The results have followed weeks of election campaigns dominated by cost of living issues and the economy, with the country's unemployment rate at its highest in a decade.

The war in the Middle East and the resulting global fuel shock have been widely blamed for the damage to New Zealand's trade-dependent economy.

The outsider who could decide next government

Support for Labour and National has fallen to historically low levels. Surveys suggest voters have lost faith in the major parties' ability to revive the sluggish economy and make the changes needed to repair ageing infrastructure.

If the National-led coalition loses its majority at the official count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would require the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, which looks likely to enter parliament for the first time.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said she would seek to negotiate with the party that secured the most seats after the official results.

Wong has said she would look to negotiate with the party that secures the most seats in parliament and that it would be possible to find common ground with National or Labour.

Qiulae Wong has been a politician for less than a year, but the 38-year-old could hold the balance of power in New Zealand's parliament. Source: AP / Jonathan Killick / Stuff

Wong, a former sustainable-business consultant, answered an advertisement for the role of head of the decade-old party and took over in November 2025.

She quickly oversaw a rebrand and a dramatic rise in Opportunity's popularity.

The party's flagship policies centre on tax: An annual NZ$19,400 ($15,685) universal basic income for most New Zealand residents funded by a 1.75 per cent annual land tax. The party also wants to simplify the country's income tax system.

National and Labour have both ruled out adopting Opportunity's tax policies.

"It might seem like we've just arrived, that this is an overnight success, but to many in this room, this result has been a long time coming," Wong told cheering supporters in Auckland on Saturday night.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press and Reuters.

title: The little-known migration story behind one of Australia's biggest Diwali celebrations
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

For the first Punjabi Sikh families who settled in Woolgoolga, Diwali was a reminder of home, of the traditions, language and familiar rituals they had left behind in India.

Far from their families and the celebrations they had grown up with, they marked the festival of lights, which celebrates the triumph of good over evil, quietly in their homes. There were no community gatherings or public festivities, just families finding small ways to keep a piece of home alive in a new country.

Deesha Maan was among the children who grew up between these two worlds.

Deesha Maan (left) arrived in Woolgoolga in 1964, but her family's ties to Australia stretch back to 1901, when her grandfather arrived in Cairns, Queensland, to work on a farm. Credit: Supplied

Just seven when she arrived in Woolgoolga in 1964, Maan remembers trading a childhood in a three-storey house in Punjab, northern India, for a life on the gravel roads and banana farms of a small coastal town, 550km north of Sydney, where she struggled to understand the language around her.

I used to hide under the table because I couldn't understand anything anyone said.

More than six decades later, Woolgoolga is home to generations of Maan's family, and the festivals once celebrated behind closed doors have become occasions for the wider community to come together.

Deesha Maan (bottom right) says she is teaching her grandkids about the same traditions that her mum taught her, but in English. Credit: SBS Punjabi

For the town's Sikh community, Diwali is also observed as Bandi Chhor Divas, commemorating the release of the sixth Sikh Guru, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, who had been imprisoned because of his faith. When Mughal emperor Jahangir granted Guru permission to leave prison, he refused to go unless the other prisoners were freed too.

The evolution of these celebrations reflects a broader story of Punjabi Sikh migration to Australia, and the generations who have built lives here while keeping their cultural and religious traditions alive.

Woolgoolga's Sikh roots

Woopie, as locals fondly call the town, is home to Australia's first Sikh gurdwara, a place of worship. Opened in June 1968, the gurdwara on Hastings Street is now listed on the NSW State Heritage Register, recognising its significance to the history of Sikh settlement in Australia.

The original gurdwara (Sikh place of worship), opened in 1968 and now heritage-listed, stands beside a new three-storey gurdwara completed in 2019. Credit: SBS Punjabi

The town's local museum traces the community's history to six pioneering Punjabi Sikh families who established themselves by the early 1950s, after Punjabi migrants arrived in the 1940s.

Some early settlers travelled on British passports, reflecting their status as British subjects under India's colonial system.

Image of the six early Punjabi settlers displayed at the town's local museum titled 'The forefathers'. Credit: SBS Punjabi

The community grew over subsequent decades, with many early migrants initially working as labourers on banana farms before moving into farming themselves.

The 2021 Census recorded 6,151 people living in Woolgoolga, of whom 1,059 identified Sikhism as their religion — over 17 per cent of the population. At least 1,000 residents reported speaking Punjabi at home.

A local road has also been named after Arkan, the surname of one of Woolgoolga's pioneering Sikh families, who went on to establish the region's second gurdwara.

Maan says the two gurdwaras in Woolgoolga serve not only the Sikh community but also welcome people from other cultural and religious backgrounds. This spirit of inclusiveness dates back to the establishment of the first gurdwara, whose inaugural management committee included three non-Sikh members of European heritage.

The inaugural committee of the first gurdwara (Sikh place of worship) also included non-Sikh members of European heritage. Credit: SBS Punjabi

"We were in fact encouraged by the Australians of European backgrounds to build this first gurdwara premises," Maan says.

Woolgoolga's Sikh farming legacy

As the news of the first-ever gurdwara in Australia spread, the Sikhs from other parts of the country began visiting Woolgoolga. Some, like Bhupinder Singh Lally, eventually decided to settle there.

Bhupinder Singh Lally's family was among the first to buy land in Woolgoolga, where they once grew bananas and now run blueberry farms. Credit: SBS Punjabi

"I remember visiting the gurdwara for the first time with my father on Christmas Day in 1968," Lally tells SBS Punjabi, recalling a moment that brought together his family's Sikh heritage and their growing connection to Australia.

Lally's grandfather and father had worked and lived in Gordonvale, Queensland. His own sons now run blueberry farms in Woolgoolga, reflecting the changing generations and agricultural livelihoods within the community. He says when his family first arrived, Indian migrants had limited opportunities to own land, making the transition from farm labour to farm ownership a significant step for many.

Despite working alongside people from different backgrounds, social acceptance took time. Lally says over time, Woolgoolga's Sikh community became a visible part of local life, with festivals such as Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas gaining wider recognition.

"Until then, we used to celebrate important events by praying under the tents," Lally says.

"Now, Diwali celebrations are at a much larger scale. Hindus, Nepali, Punjabis, we all celebrate together."

But what makes these occasions particularly special, Lally says, is the way Punjabi traditions have blended with the Australian way of life.

It is a sentiment echoed by others in the community.

Satpal Singh is a descendant of a pioneering Punjabi Sikh family that settled in Woolgoolga in the 1940s. Credit: SBS Punjabi

For Satpal Singh, a member of one of the pioneering Sikh families in Woolgoolga, the growth of these celebrations is also a reflection of how the community has held on to its cultural roots across generations.

"Woolgoolga is a bit time-locked in that sense that the Punjab our ancestors brought with them, we still carry it forward," he tells SBS Punjabi.

He has witnessed Diwali evolve from a festival barely acknowledged in the region to now being introduced to children at local schools.

Yet for him, preserving one's heritage has never meant being any less Australian.

I don't think my life would be complete without things that Australia has given me. But I'm still deep-rooted in my own faith, so I am an Australian Sikh.

title: Australia's biggest cultural project since the Opera House goes live
text:
IN BRIEF NSW Premier Chris Minns and Arts Minister John Graham officially opened the Powerhouse Parramatta on Saturday.

An opening festival running over three weeks and four weekends will feature 179 events, most of which are free.

After almost 15 years, the doors of Australia's newest museum, Powerhouse Parramatta, are officially open to the public.

The billion-dollar museum has been described as the largest cultural infrastructure project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House.

About 3,000 objects are on display across 18,000 square metres of exhibition and public space, making it the state's largest museum. On its opening weekend, 25,000 visitors have registered to attend events.

The museum's interim CEO, Abbie Galvin, has said it's wonderful to see the project finally completed.

"It is now a building that is for the community of Western Sydney, the community of New South Wales and of course, Australia," she said. "It is an incredible cultural institution."

"And it represents innovation. It represents education. And it absolutely represents wonderment."

NSW Premier Chris Minns and Arts Minister John Graham opened the riverfront building on Saturday, saying it would be a magnet for Australians looking to spend time engaging with science and culture for free.

Some of the museum's exhibitions do, however, have an entry fee.

Powerhouse Parramatta's opening festival program will run until 29 November. Credit: Powerhouse Studios

Minns also credited former Coalition premier Mike Baird for starting the project, telling reporters that his party had been wrongly critical of it when in opposition.

"We were wrong," Minns said. "This is fantastic. This is going to be great for Western Sydney. It's going to be great for NSW," he said.

The Opposition, too, was keen to highlight its contribution.

"Western Sydney has been waiting for its fair share and the Liberals and Nationals have delivered. If Labor had won the election in either 2015 or 2019, Powerhouse Parramatta would not be here today," it said in a joint statement.

Powerhouse Parramatta to become global destination

The striking building is covered in a lattice of 1,300 individual steel pieces and is the first public building in Australia to be awarded six green stars under the Green Building Council of Australia's new rating system.

It has a 24-hour accessible outdoor space with gardens, amphitheatres, and promenades linking the Parramatta River to Phillip Street.

An opening festival program over three weeks and four weekends will feature 179 events, most of which are free, across First Nations culture, science and technology, design, music, film, and food.

Acclaimed British artist Es Devlin, whose works are part of the opening exhibitions, has said she thinks the new museum will become a global destination.

Es Devlin's The Turning installation is one of Powerhouse Parramatta's opening exhibitions. Credit: Powerhouse Studios

"It's the first time that the building gets to sing," she told ABC radio about the opening.

"It's almost like the builders have been crafting this Stradivarius [violin] for seven years, and now is the first time it's given its voice and it meets its public.

"This one is really in a class of its own."

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the opening day of the Powerhouse Parramatta was "packed", with crowds and queues for each of the five opening exhibitions.

Attendees have described the building as "instantly iconic" and said that, despite the long wait and the political battles over it, the new Powerhouse appears to have been worth it.

Powerhouse Parramatta's predecessor, Powerhouse Ultimo, is undergoing a $300 million heritage restoration and rebuild project on its 1988 structure. While it too has been delayed by controversies and budget blowouts, it is anticipated to open in late 2028 or early 2029.

title: The grim news for Australian travellers quietly updated this week
text:
In brief Qantas said this week that it would continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to higher fuel costs.

Meanwhile, Westpac has said a surprising number of Australians are ahead on their mortgage repayments.

Australians could soon face higher airfares and fewer flights as Qantas responds to rising fuel costs. Meanwhile, shoppers hoping for big bargains as David Jones enters voluntary administration could be left disappointed.

And as interest rates rise again, new figures reveal just how far ahead some borrowers are on their repayments.

Qantas airfares to rise

Australians love to travel, but they'll soon have to pay even more for the privilege.

In a market update issued this week, Qantas said it would continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to higher fuel costs.

That means more expensive tickets for consumers, and fewer flights to choose from on certain routes. The cuts will be coming from its domestic operations.

However, it would appear that more recent price increases haven't deterred Qantas' customers, with the company saying demand remains resilient.

The carrier said international demand across its Qantas and Jetstar brands remains strong, with flyers redirecting travel away from the Middle East.

Of course, those international jaunts may give travellers something to think about, depending on their destination.

The Australian dollar lost around 2 per cent over the week, roughing up the exchange rate for certain popular holiday spots.

David Jones bargains uncertain

It's quite common for retailers entering voluntary administration to hold major sales and offload some excess inventory, but it might be a little different for David Jones — there could be less to sell.

This week, the iconic Australian department store called in a team to manage the business after it wound up in financial trouble.

However, as University of Technology retail expert Gary Mortimer told SBS' On the Money Podcast, David Jones operates a largely concession-based model under which brands retain control.

"They own that space, they own that inventory, they own that staff," Mortimer said.

READ MORE How David Jones could emerge from administration a very different retailer

"It's likely those brands will go in and collect that inventory whilst they can and move it to their physical store assets."

The administrators are now working through restructuring options, including the closure of some stores. That's where some bargains may ultimately be found.

"If it's a David Jones' branded product, you'd expect to see either some discounting or ideally maybe moving that inventory to stores that will be retained," Mortimer said.

David Jones is the world's oldest continuously running department store still operating under the same name.

Are you ahead on your repayments?

While the Reserve Bank's fifth interest-rate hike of the year will be painful for many, it would appear there are some borrowers who may be able to absorb that increase.

This week, Westpac revealed 37 per cent of its customers are more than two years ahead on their repayments.

In fact, 53 per cent have buffers of six months at the very least. Just 1 per cent of customers are behind.

Nevertheless, this week's RBA rate rise will likely add $107 per month to the repayments of a typical $700,000 loan over 25 years.

The big four banks will pass on their new rates on Black Friday — which, perhaps somewhat ironically, is also Friday the 13th.

title: Chris v Chris: What to know about New Zealand's tightly wedged election
text:
In Brief Chris Luxon and Chris Hipkins are locked in a tight race to lead New Zealand's next government.

Minor parties could hold the balance of power in an election expected to be too close to call.

Across the Tasman, New Zealanders are preparing to head to the polls in what is shaping up to be a tightly contested election.

It will be a battle of two Chrises.

In one corner is Christopher Luxon, the current prime minister and leader of the centre-right National Party, who is seeking a second term leading his coalition government.

In the other is Chris Hipkins, the leader of the centre-left Labour Party, who briefly served as prime minister after Jacinda Ardern resigned in 2023 before losing office later that year.

With campaigning now wrapped up, New Zealanders will vote on Saturday 7 November to decide who forms the country's next government.

Here's what you need to know.

Who are the two main players?

Chris Luxon, National Party

Luxon is New Zealand's current prime minister and has led the country since 2023.

The former Air New Zealand chief executive led the centre-right National Party back into government after defeating Labour three years ago.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is hoping for a second term under his conservative coalition. Source: AAP / Ben Mckay

His campaign has focused heavily on the economy, including plans to return the budget to surplus and expand New Zealand's KiwiSaver retirement scheme.

But his first term has been turbulent. Luxon survived two confidence votes from National MPs this year amid weak polling, economic pressure and tensions within his governing coalition.

Chris Hipkins, Labour

Hipkins is seeking to return Labour to government three years after its election defeat.

The 48-year-old became prime minister in January 2023 following Jacinda Ardern's resignation, but served for less than a year before losing office at the October election.

Since then, he has campaigned on cost of living relief, stronger public services and investment in housing, infrastructure and healthcare.

Former New Zealand prime minister Chris Hipkins is hoping to get back into the top job after losing power in 2023. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

How do New Zealand elections work?

New Zealand uses what's known as a mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system.

Voters cast two votes: one for their local electorate representative and one for the political party they want to govern.

People of Māori descent can choose whether to enrol on the general electoral roll or the Māori electoral roll.

Parliament is usually made up of 120 seats. Seventy-one are elected from geographic electorates, including seven Māori electorates, while the remainder are allocated according to each party's share of the nationwide vote.

A party generally needs at least 5 per cent of the party vote, or to win an electorate seat, to enter parliament.

Because seats are allocated proportionally, it is uncommon for a single party to win an outright majority.

That means coalition governments are the norm.

Every government since MMP was introduced in 1996 has relied on support from smaller parties, with the exception of Jacinda Ardern's Labour government in 2020.

Why the minor parties could decide the result

While much of the attention has focused on Luxon and Hipkins, smaller parties could ultimately determine who forms the next government.

Polling suggests neither National nor Labour is likely to win enough seats to govern alone, making coalition negotiations crucial.

These are the parties likely to play a major role:

New Zealand First: Led by veteran politician Winston Peters, the right-wing populist party is campaigning on issues including immigration, energy prices and withdrawing from the Paris climate agreement.

ACT : Led by deputy prime minister David Seymour, the libertarian-leaning party has focused on immigration, crime and reducing the size of government.

The Greens: Labour's most likely coalition partner, campaigning on climate action, tax reform and cost-of-living measures, including a proposed wealth tax.

Te Pāti Māori: Focused on Māori rights and representation, and expected to retain several Māori electorates.

Opportunity (TOP) : A centrist party led by Qiulae Wong that has never won a seat in parliament but is hovering around the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter parliament and could become a kingmaker.

What are the main issues for voters?

Like many countries around the world, the cost of living remains New Zealand's top election issue.

Inflation has eased from earlier highs, but households continue to face pressure from petrol prices, housing costs and everyday expenses.

The country's unemployment rate has risen to 5.7 per cent, its highest level in 11 years, while economic growth has remained sluggish following a prolonged downturn.

Healthcare has also emerged as a major campaign issue amid concerns about strained hospitals, staffing shortages and long waiting times for treatment.

Housing affordability remains a longstanding problem, particularly for younger New Zealanders trying to enter the property market.

Immigration, government spending, climate policy and Māori issues have also featured prominently throughout the campaign.

What's at stake on Indigenous issues?

The election comes after years of heated debate about Māori rights and representation, particularly around the Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand's founding agreement between Māori leaders and the British Crown.

The coalition government has rolled back several policies designed to give Māori greater representation in public decision-making, while ACT has campaigned against what it calls "race-based" policies and has proposed abolishing the Waitangi Tribunal.

Meanwhile, Te Pāti Māori has sought to mobilise Indigenous voters and frame the election as a pivotal moment for Māori representation.

Because the overall contest is so close, the outcome in the seven Māori electorates could also influence coalition negotiations after election day.

What does the polling indicate?

Most polls suggest the race is too close to call.

The latest poll from Post-Freshwater Strategy, released on Friday, placed the opposition Labour Party slightly ahead, but still with no clear outcome for the election.

But it also placed the Opportunity Party at 5.1 per cent — just above the threshold for representation in parliament. If it crosses that line, it could emerge as a kingmaker in coalition talks.

Another October poll from Roy Morgan placed the centre-right bloc of National, ACT and NZ First as holding a narrow lead over Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori.

Another poll by Infrastructure New Zealand, an industry association, released on Friday, put Labour at 30.7 per cent and National at 26.4 per cent.

Analysts have also noted growing support for smaller parties, reflecting frustration among some voters with New Zealand's two major parties.

When is New Zealand's election and when will we know the results?

New Zealanders will head to the polls on Saturday 7 November, with voting closing at 7pm local time (5pm AEDT).

More than 1.4 million votes had already been cast during advance voting by the middle of election week.

Early results are expected to start emerging shortly after polls close, but New Zealand may not know who will form government on election night.

If no party wins enough seats to govern outright, major parties will need to negotiate coalition or support agreements with smaller parties, a process that can take days or even weeks.

That places the centrist Opportunity Party in a unique position. The party says it is willing to work with either side of politics and, if it enters parliament, could have significant influence over who forms New Zealand's next government.

What is clear, however, is that whichever major party wins the most votes is likely to need support from at least one smaller party, meaning coalition negotiations could ultimately decide who becomes New Zealand's next prime minister.

Almost half-a-million Brisbane residents could receive scheduled respite from aircraft noise under a new package of flightpath changes released for public consultation, but Airservices Australia has discarded two other options its own consultants found were technically viable. Airservices announced five options for community consultation on Monday as part of the final package of the Noise Action Plan for Brisbane Airport, saying the proposals could provide periods of respite from aircraft arrivals for about 482,000 residents – and reduce aircraft noise for a further 139,000 – through higher altitudes and smoother descents. Airservices Australia is exploring ways to lesson the impact of aircraft noise from Brisbane Airport operations. Brisbane Airport “The options we are presenting provide a real opportunity for noise improvements for some of the communities we have most frequently engaged with throughout the Noise Action Plan for Brisbane,” Airservices Australia program delivery head Donna Marshall said. “New runway-aligned communities, who are subject to both arrival and departure operations, could receive respite from arrivals in between peak traffic periods on an alternating basis with legacy runway communities.

Advertisement

“Communities to the north and west of the airport, who are overflown by aircraft arriving to the new runway, could also experience lower noise levels from the increased flightpath altitudes and smoother descent profiles. Some of these communities could also benefit from respite options.” The options emerged from a detailed review by aviation consultancy Trax International, which examined Brisbane’s complex airspace system and assessed 17 concepts aimed at reducing the impact of aircraft noise on surrounding communities. Related Article Perspective

Brisbane Airport Is a noisy sky simply the price you pay for living in a thriving city? But while the Trax report identified seven concepts as viable for further consideration, Airservices ultimately narrowed that list to five, despite the remaining two concepts being found technically feasible. The five options out for public consultation include two noise-sharing runway operation concepts and three arrival flightpath changes designed to keep aircraft higher over residential areas for longer.

Advertisement

One proposal would give some Brisbane suburbs regular breaks from aircraft arriving overhead. On days when winds came from the north, planes would be directed to just one runway for arrivals, giving those under the other runway’s flightpaths respite. Airservices estimated the arrangement could be used on about 100 weekdays a year when traffic and weather conditions allowed. Related Article Brisbane Airport Airport noise costs Brisbane $100m a year, curfew would cost $10m, report claims A second proposal would extend those respite periods by allowing more departing aircraft to use over-water runway ends, potentially delaying the need to return to normal runway operations. The remaining proposals focus on making aircraft quieter by keeping them higher above suburbs as they approach Brisbane Airport. One would allow planes arriving from the south and east at night to remain hundreds of metres higher over existing flight paths, benefiting about 50,000 residents. Another would do the same for nighttime arrivals from the north and west, while a third would permanently raise aircraft altitudes on several arrival routes from the north and west during both day and night operations. Aircraft would also spend less time flying level over populated areas, reducing noise on the ground.

Advertisement

But the most contentious finding in the report may be what has not been put before the public. Trax found viable a broader noise-sharing concept, known as Concept 10, that would have provided predictable respite in both northerly and southerly wind conditions by alternating all four of Brisbane Airport’s segregated runway modes. The report found it would offer the most comprehensive respite arrangement and could operate regardless of wind direction. Airservices rejected the proposal after concluding the new departure routes required to make it work would newly affect about 136,000 residents, including people in Coorparoo, Holland Park, Salisbury, Macgregor, Parkinson, Browns Plains, Regents Park and Boronia Heights. South-east Queensland’s congested airspace. Airservices Australia The report estimated about 198,700 people would be exposed to aircraft noise events above 60 decibels beneath one proposed new route, compared with about 41,700 beneath the existing path.

Advertisement

Another proposal would have diverted some non-jet aircraft onto a new approach path from the north. Airservices rejected the idea, finding it would affect about 70,000 residents while delivering benefits for only a handful of flights. Trax found there was “little uncommitted airspace” in south-east Queensland, with Brisbane operations constrained by Defence airspace around Amberley and offshore training areas, airports at the Gold and Sunshine coasts, general aviation operations at Archerfield and existing air traffic control systems. Trax examined seven broader airspace redesign concepts, including rerouting departures over Moreton Bay, using Amberley airspace for civil arrivals and relocating Sunshine Coast traffic to improve Brisbane operations. None were considered viable. Public consultation on the five shortlisted options will run until December 13, after which Airservices planned to determine whether any proposals should proceed. TMK Energy has notched up a double win at its wholly-owned Gurvantes XXXV coal seam gas project in Mongolia, smashing another monthly production record and securing regulatory acceptance of its declaration of (gas) discovery, putting it firmly on the path to a potential 30-year production licence. The dual achievements come as the company kicks off a new drilling and well enhancement campaign designed to push the project towards commerciality. The company says average daily gas production for October jumped 11 per cent to 971 cubic metres per day (m³/day), up from 872m³/day in September. TMK Energy prepares for well re-completions at its recently declared Lucky Fox gas discovery within the Gurvantes XXXV project in Mongolia. The October record of 34,300 standard cubic feet per day came without any contribution from new wells, with field uptime remaining high despite brief power cuts and water production holding steady at 410 barrels daily. At the seven-well Lucky Fox pilot in the Nariin Sukhait coal district, TMK is pumping water from the coal seams to lower reservoir pressure and coax trapped methane into flowing, a process known as “desorption”. Management sees the rising gas rates against steady water output as a strong sign its reservoir strategy is hitting the mark.

Advertisement

‘The Company remains fully funded for the 2026 work program and is continuing towards its target of proving commerciality of the project.’ TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson Plenty is riding on that success. Spanning 8400 square kilometres of Mongolia’s South Gobi Basin, Gurvantes XXXV boasts an independently certified 2C contingent resource of 1.2 trillion cubic feet of gas (Tcf) already discovered but not yet commercially developed. Another 5.3Tcf of prospective resources adds serious exploration upside. A drilling rig and workover rig are now on site, giving TMK the firepower to kick its gas ambitions up another gear. And rather than splash out on a swag of new wells, the company is looking to squeeze more gas from its existing producers through a lower-cost re-completion program. TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson said: “With the 2026 Work Program now underway, we expect to see further significant increases in gas production rates over the next few months as both LF-08 is brought into production and the three well re-completions are undertaken.” Following equipment-delivery delays, the campaign kicked off in October with the cleanout of idle well LF-03, setting the stage for the first of three planned re-completions. The next step is to spud its latest well, Lucky Fox-08 (LF-08). The field campaign is scheduled to wrap up in November, with the new well slated to be producing by mid-December.

Advertisement

TMK also plans to temporarily shut in LF-02, its second-best producer, for a pressure build-up test during nearby drilling. While the pause could take some shine off November’s production figures, it should provide valuable data on reservoir depressurisation while protecting the well from further damage. Looking further ahead, the company has flagged additional drilling in 2027 to test the wider resource and support development planning. If the current re-completions deliver the goods, the technique could be rolled out across the remaining Lucky Fox wells, giving TMK another cost-effective lever to lift gas flows. Adding to the project’s credentials, the company is pushing ahead with a proposed one-megawatt gas-to-power plant at site alongside local partner Dashvaanjil Group, with engineering and costings complete. A final investment decision has shifted to the first quarter of 2027, allowing fresh production data to guide engine sizing and help avoid excess flaring. The plant could power TMK’s operations and nearby industrial customers. The bigger prize could lie just across the border in China. Coal supplies 85 per cent of Mongolia’s primary energy. However, Gurvantes sits less than 20km from the Chinese border, putting TMK on the doorstep of one of the world’s biggest gas markets. Rising demand and a preference for local gas supplies and pipeline imports over pricier seaborne liquefied natural gas (LNG) could give it a valuable commercial edge. On the regulatory front, TMK has 90 days to lodge and agree an appraisal program with Mongolia’s Mineral Resources and Petroleum Authority, paving the way for at least 180 days of extended production testing. The results will underpin initial gas reserves and a field development plan, bringing a 30-year exploitation licence with a possible five-year extension, another step closer.

Armed with record gas flows, a key regulatory milestone and a capital-savvy drilling program now spinning the rods, TMK is edging closer to proving it can consistently and economically extract gas from its sizeable Mongolian resource. If the next round of wells delivers the goods, the company could be sitting on the makings of a long-term energy business with a potentially lucrative export market just a stone’s throw away. Dalaroo Metals has delivered another significant gold intersection at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire, West Africa, hitting a 13-metre-thick zone of mineralisation grading 2.67 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 87m depth. The interval, at its fresh Wilfred prospect, also included a higher-grade six-metre core running at 4.19g/t gold from 87m and is just 1.25 kilometres along strike from its recent high-grade Fournier discovery. Other intercepts in the same hole include 7m going 0.84g/t gold from 63m, 6m assaying 0.78g/t gold from 78m and a deep single-metre interval grading 16.2g/t from 187m. Dalaroo Metals’ diamond drill pad set up ready for follow-up drilling at its high-grade West African Fournier gold discovery. The latest headline hit at the Wilfred prospect confirms that the company’s spectacular maiden discovery hole at Fournier last month was no flash in the pan. The Fournier discovery comprises results from two opposing holes drilled to more than 200m depth as part of Dalaroo’s maiden reverse circulation (RC) drilling orientation program at the project. The scissored holes were the first drilling undertaken across the seven-kilometre-long Gold Ridge target corridor. One of those two holes returned a headline hit of 18m at 7.31g/t gold from 63m and a second, deeper zone of 16m at 1.46g/t gold from 113m. The opposing hole, collared 43m northeast of the headline hole, also gave up a healthy 23-metre intercept assaying 2.14g/t gold from surface.

Advertisement

’What is particularly encouraging is the occurrence of significant gold mineralisation at widely separated locations.” Dalaroo Metals managing director John Morgan Now, with a similar style of mineralisation appearing 1.25km away on the northernmost Wilfred section - directly along strike from Fournier - Dalaroo believes it could be on the cusp of defining a potentially significant mineralised corridor. For explorers, geological consistency is a major tick in the box when working to prove up a large-scale, economic deposit. It suggests a predictable and potentially extensive system. Dalaroo says that while its results so far show meaningful gold grades and widths at the two widely separated locations, mineralisation continuity between sections has not yet been established. However, Dalaroo says the similarity of alteration, quartz-sulphide veining and prospective host rocks at the two locations supports its working model of a possibly uniform and major structurally controlled gold system. Dalaroo Metals managing director John Morgan said: “The intersection of a new zone of significant gold mineralisation at the Wilfred Prospect, 1.25km from the Fournier discovery hole, is an excellent result and strongly supports our view that a large mineralised system is present at Bondoukou. We are very encouraged by the fact that the results from the first two prospects drilled at the Bondoukou Gold Ridge have both delivered significant gold intercepts from our maiden drilling program.”

Advertisement

Encouraged by the latest results and with growing promise of potentially bigger things ahead, the company says it’s moving immediately to crank up an expanded 1750-metre diamond drilling program, alongside preparations for a major induced polarisation (IP) geophysical survey. The Wilfred and Fournier prospects are both situated on the 40-kilometre-long Bondoukou Gold Ridge, a major regional structure which has seen little modern exploration. Dalaroo’s early maiden drilling successes suggest the entire ridge could be highly prospective for further gold discoveries. With its apparently persistent, open-ended mineralisation along strike and at depth, the Wilfred area offers an abundance of immediate follow-up drill targets. That 1.25-kilometre-long stretch of untested ground between Fournier and Wilfred now looms as a high-priority target zone for Dalaroo. Any success in connecting the two prospects could quickly elevate the scale of the company’s find. Dalaroo’s maiden drilling program at Bondoukou represents the first ever drilling put into the ground and it has already thrown up two significant gold discoveries at two separate but potentially structurally-linked prospects, returning significant gold intercepts in eight of the twelve holes reported to date. The company appears well-funded to accelerate its exploration plans, reporting a cash position of $3.1 million at the end of the recent October quarter.

Singapore Airlines’ overhaul of its business class seats has triggered a social media backlash from potential travellers who are taking aim at the “progressive” look for not being in sync with the iconic brand. Critics argue the carrier has abandoned its traditional deep blues, golds and oranges in its top-tier seating in favour of an off-brand mineral grey and bright yellow palate. “Like a suit with a sneaker”: the new Singapore Airlines business class seat. Chris Zappone While the seating itself appears slick and functional, the new colour scheme is drawing significant criticism across social media, with one user posting: “Last chance to fly Singapore Airlines before they make it ugly.” In a jab to the global design group commissioned to upgrade the airline’s business livery, another said: “It’s really European and does not align with Singapore values.” Another claimed: “A Singaporean designer would’ve done much better.”

Advertisement

Julia de Bono, the CEO from BMW Designworks, the company hired by Singapore Airlines to design the seat, said “the palette was deliberate”. She said the “warmer” look had “served the airline for a long time, and many of the cabins are going warm and more traditional right now”. “But we wanted this business class to stand on its own, with its own attitude modern, progressive, and refreshing.” US-based de Bono told an audience of journalists that: “We wanted the cabin to feel high-tech, luxurious, and future-forward. Mineral greys – you see them everywhere right now – they are really having this balance and stable feel to them.”

Advertisement

The new Singapore Airlines business class seat. Chris Zappone In the refresh, the premium economy seats are a warm grey-blue, with orange accents, while economy seats are blue with grey trim. In a separate interview, de Bono described the colour design as being “like a suit with a sneaker … modern and fresh”. Related Article Aviation $2b and plenty of new seats: Inside airlines’ battle for first-class supremacy The verdict from the public was distinctly less forgiving. Singapore-based Radha K, the head of marketing for a tech company, said the “colours for the new business class seats doesn’t match Singapore Airline’s unique brand look and feel”.

Advertisement

“The new design doesn’t elevate the brand look … it makes Singapore Airlines look like they are having an identity crisis,” she said. There is also an undercurrent of national identity for an airline that is closely associated with the nation. One Singapore-based commenter wrote: “If you get a non-Singaporean who [does] not live the culture, the essence[,] and appreciate the legacy of [Singapore Airlines] this is what you get. A downgrade.” Current, Singapore Airlines business class seating on an A380. Getty Images Malaysia-Australian author Kean Wong said Singapore Airlines is “one of the state’s key talismans”, like the nation’s extensive public housing system, schools and sovereign wealth funds. “So it’s no surprise that there’s objection to the striking yellow rather than a ‘native’ or a deeper tropical colour.”

Advertisement

Wong said the yellow also has a ‘budget streak’ quality to it, a la Scoot airlines, the low-cost carrier owned by Singapore Airlines, a sentiment shared by people on social media. Shukor Yusof, founder of Singapore-based aviation consultancy Endau Analytics, said: “I’ve been monitoring the reactions: it’s been mixed. Can’t please everyone! “The seats may be rather bland to some, but I suspect it won’t hurt the bottom line at all,” he said. Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience Ong Wah Li said the business class seat “has been designed to offer a fresh and contemporary take on premium travel … that reflects a modern, progressive, and forward-looking design philosophy.” “While Singapore Airline’s signature warm and classic aesthetic has served us well over the years, we wanted this new product to have its own character, combining a refreshing aesthetic with a sense of sophistication and understated luxury,” said Ong.

“We do not subscribe to a fixed colour palette across our cabins.” The Singapore Airlines refit was announced in 2024 with expectations the first of its A350-900 planes would be ready by this year. Delays mean the first refit planes won’t enter service until the second half of 2027.

International Rugby League chairman Troy Grant has defended the decision to permit players to represent the nation where one of their great-grandparents were born, as Samoa forward Spencer Leniu lashed out at World Cup organisers, claiming “they’ve used our people to sell games”. The new eligibility rules were announced in Sydney on Monday as the Pacific and the United States were confirmed as the host of the next World Cup in 2030. Loading Leniu said holding the next edition in the region “shows the importance of our people in growing our game”, but took a shot at the huge gulf in player payments at this World Cup as he was hit with a grade-three charge over an incident that led him to be sin-binned during Samoa’s 44-12 semi-final defeat to Australia on Sunday night. “Let’s be honest, our little nations carried this WC. Yet we are paid $850 a game [compared] to the Aussies [who get] 30/40k for the tournament,” Leniu wrote in a social media post.

Advertisement

He is facing a two-game suspension, which would rule him out of Parramatta’s NRL opener in Las Vegas next season, after being hit with a contrary conduct charge for making a gesture towards referee Adam Gee. The incoming Parramatta enforcer said it was “no secret that they’ve used our people to sell games” and believes they should be properly rewarded for it. Samoan supporters make their presence felt during Sunday night’s World Cup semi-final against Australia at Allianz Stadium. Getty Images Members of the Australian team receive $40,000 each for the World Cup under the Rugby League Players’ Association’s collective bargaining agreement with the Australian Rugby League Commission, while players from other countries have received $850. “Taking the next WC to the US, specifically Utah and Hawaii, where there is a big Polynesian community shows the importance of our people in growing our game,” Leniu said. “So I believe if they are going to use that as a tool to generate money, our little nations should be compensated fairly for it.”

Advertisement

The ARL Commission will organise and run the 2030 tournament, which will be staged in a Magic Round-style format with a full slate of men’s and women’s pool matches to be played over three days in one stadium before moving onto another venue. Under the format, the group stage will take place at up to five venues from Australia to the US, with potential host cities and states including Sydney, Brisbane, Auckland, Hawaii and Utah. Spencer Leniu is facing a two match ban for making a gesture towards referee Adam Gee. Getty Images The latest change to rugby league’s eligibility criteria continues its fluid approach to regulations governing the international game and was the result of an application from the Cook Islands and their coach, Karmichael Hunt. While payers have previously been allowed to wear the colours of a country where one of their parents or grandparents was born, they can now point to the nation of birth of one of their eight great-grandparents.

Advertisement

Sport governing bodies such as World Rugby, FIFA and World Athletics also have a grandparent rule. But the IRL’s extension to another generation in a player’s lineage puts the code in a league of its own. Raiders fullback Kaeo Weekes will be able to represent the Cook Islands under new eligibility rules. Getty Images “It may not be as pure as some people may think it should be, or fit their mindsets. I don’t really care about that,” said Grant, a former NSW racing minister. “I care about growing the game and giving every player the opportunity to represent their nation and I care that the fans are getting the best outcomes, which we have seen during this World Cup.”

Advertisement

International rugby league has enjoyed the fruits of players embracing their heritage, particularly those from Pacific Island backgrounds. Tonga and Samoa, who met in an unforgettable pool game at CommBank Stadium eight days ago, have become heavyweights as a result. The new move is a shameless bid to spread even more NRL talent around the globe, no matter how distant the connection between players and the nation of their forebears. Luke Keary in action for Ireland at the 2022 World Cup. He qualified for the country via his paternal grandfather. Getty Images Grant cited Canberra fullback Kaeo Weekes as a player who could benefit from the updated rules, saying they would have allowed him to turn out for the Cook Islands at this World Cup if they had been in place before the tournament. “I think we have players sitting on the sidelines who the public deserve to see show their skills,” Grant said.

Environment Minister Murray Watt has admitted Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s ordinarily united team has been leaking and undermining Treasurer Jim Chalmers, and appealed for it to stop. Environment Minister Murray Watt. Labor has pointed to higher fuel prices sparked by America’s war with Iran, which the RBA acknowledges has made the inflation problem much worse. Asked if he believed it was clear that colleagues were undermining Chalmers, Watt added: “Well, I think it’s pretty obvious that there’s all sorts of people making all sorts of comments.

“Many of the features that are impacting on our economy are of course well outside any treasurer’s control, and I very much support Jim Chalmers in his efforts.” This masthead reported last month that MPs believed the critique of Chalmers was driven by a combination of genuine concern about Labor’s near record spending level, ideological opponents in the media, normal midterm grumbles and factional gripes from Chalmers’ internal critics. Speaking on the Inside Politics podcast two weeks ago, Chalmers issued somewhat of a mea culpa after weeks of bruising media coverage. Labor has promised to find savings in the December budget update, but it is pressured to create net savings, which outweigh new spending. Labor could alternatively raise taxes to dampen inflation, though voters often punish governments for tax hikes. The prime minister claimed on Monday that he would be able to tell voters at the next election that “unlike most of the advanced economies, we haven’t had a single quarter of negative growth.” While Australia has not suffered decline in nominal growth due to high levels of migration, growth per person has declined over several quarters since Labor came to power in 2022.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.
